evidence.snippet: These findings gave rise to genetic analysis of the hALG11 cDNA, in which homozygosity for mutation c.T257C (p.L86S) was identified.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the homozygous index allele.

evidence.snippet: Subsequent ALG11 gene deletion/duplication analysis found a paternally inherited whole gene deletion of ALG11 in the patient.
evidence.explanation: Documents a structural allele paired with the maternal p.Leu46Pro variant.

steps/1.description: Homozygous or compound heterozygous ALG11 variants impair gene function. Missense alleles, frameshift and splice-site variants, and a whole-gene deletion in trans with a missense allele have been reported. Functional effects differ by allele.

evidence.snippet: Determination of mannosyltransferase activities of early steps of lipid-linked oligosaccharide biosynthesis in fibroblasts indicated that the patient was deficient in elongating Man3GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol.
evidence.explanation: Direct assay of the elongation defect in index patient fibroblasts.

evidence.snippet: Immunofluorescence examinations combined with western blotting showed no differences of intracellular localization or expression of ALG11 between control and patient fibroblasts, respectively, indicating no mislocalization or degradation of the mutated transferase.
evidence.explanation: Preserved measured abundance and localization apply to the index allele, not all disease-associated alleles.

steps/2.description: ALG11 activity is deficient at the fourth and fifth mannose-transfer steps of lipid-linked oligosaccharide assembly. The p.Leu86Ser index fibroblasts had impaired elongation despite unchanged measured protein abundance and localization. This catalytic phenotype should not be generalized to the abundance of every ALG11 variant.

evidence.snippet: As expected, patient 2 had slightly less ALG11 protein due to the paternally inherited whole gene deletion (Figure 2).
evidence.explanation: Directly reports lower protein abundance in this genotype.

steps/3.description: Reduced steady-state ALG11 protein is an allele-dependent observation. It was reported in fibroblasts with a whole-gene deletion in trans with p.Leu46Pro. Other tested missense genotypes had normal measured abundance. Reduced abundance alone does not establish an altered protein-degradation rate.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of dolichol-linked oligosaccharides in patient-derived fibroblasts revealed an accumulation of Man3GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol and Man4GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the two LLO species that accumulate, fixing the exact step of the assembly block.

evidence.snippet: who presented an accumulation of shortened dolichol-linked oligosaccharides leading to CDG-Ip (ALG11-CDG)
evidence.explanation: Independently confirms shortened LLO accumulation as the biochemical signature of the disorder.

steps/4.description: Shortened Man3GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol and Man4GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol accumulate in affected fibroblasts. This is impaired precursor assembly rather than proof that every LLO molecule is arrested or that those truncated species are transferred unchanged to proteins.

evidence.snippet: The isoelectric focusing pattern of the patient's serum transferrin showed the partial loss of complete N-glycan side chains, which is a characteristic sign for CDG-I.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates hypoglycosylation of a serum glycoprotein in the index patient.

evidence.snippet: Fibroblasts from the skin punch biopsy also yielded abnormally truncated GP130 isoforms on western blot
evidence.explanation: Documents the cellular glycoprotein readout.

evidence.snippet: Interestingly, serum N-glycan analysis and carbohydrate deficient transferrin were normal, but the novel GP130 biomarker revealed cellular hypoglycosylation, while LLO analysis was consistent with ALG11-CDG.
evidence.explanation: Supports coexistence of normal serum screening and abnormal cellular glycosylation.

steps/5.description: Protein N-glycosylation is reduced. The index serum transferrin pattern reflected loss of complete N-glycan side chains, and affected fibroblasts show lower-molecular-weight GP130 glycoforms. These are protein- and sample-specific readouts: normal serum transferrin does not exclude a cellular defect. Comparative diagnostic sensitivity of GP130 versus transferrin has not been established.

evidence.snippet: During the 3.5 week interval from the fetal MRI to the postnatal brain MRI, the brain did not increase in size indicating an arrested growth pattern. This should be differentiated from a decrease in size, or atrophy, which did not occur during that same time period.
evidence.explanation: Explicitly distinguishes developmental growth arrest from atrophy in this child.

steps/6.description: In one molecularly and biochemically characterized child, fetal brain growth arrested after normal mid-gestation biometry. The fetal-to-neonatal MRI interval showed absent growth rather than measured tissue loss. The cellular mechanism connecting ALG11 dysfunction to this developmental phenotype is unknown.

evidence.snippet: There was near complete loss of cerebral hemispheres, severe cerebellar atrophy, and decreased volume of the brainstem.
evidence.explanation: Documents the extent of structural loss at age seven in a serially imaged patient.

evidence.snippet: Progressive cerebral atrophy, hypomyelination and corpus callosum hypoplasia were striking features in brain MRI images taken during our follow-up.
evidence.explanation: Independently reports the same progressive atrophy with hypomyelination in a different patient.

evidence.snippet: Both MRI and CT scan of the brain were within normal limits, but the EEG was abnormal.
evidence.explanation: Qualifies the spectrum: the 14-year-old patient did not have the same structural imaging phenotype.

steps/7.description: Serial MRI has documented progressive cerebral tissue loss in several severe cases. The child with prenatal growth arrest later had near-complete cerebral hemispheric loss and severe cerebellar and brainstem volume loss at age seven. That sequence is an individual longitudinal observation, not an obligatory course for all ALG11-CDG; another reported adolescent had normal MRI and CT.

treatments/6.description: Confirm parental variants and discuss autosomal recessive recurrence, testing of relatives, and reproductive options. When both parents carry the causal alleles, each pregnancy has a 25% chance of an affected child. Prenatal or preimplantation testing can be discussed once familial variants are known; counseling remains nondirective.

open_questions/0.rationale: Unremarkable pregnancies in earlier patients and fetal brain growth arrest in a later child represent clinical variability rather than conflicting observations. In that child, fetal-to-neonatal MRI showed absent growth, whereas later follow-up documented marked tissue loss. The prevalence of prenatal onset, genotype associations and cellular basis remain unresolved.

open_questions/1.rationale: The proposed otoneurotoxicity of cytosolic LLO intermediates is a hypothesis from the clinical literature. Neither the cited patient studies nor their fibroblast assays establish accumulation in the inner ear or a causal cochlear injury pathway. Similar hearing impairment in RFT1-CDG motivates comparison but does not prove a shared toxic substrate.

open_questions/2.rationale: Truncated LLO and GP130 hypoglycosylation are reproducible fibroblast observations. They do not directly demonstrate GP130 signaling failure, ER stress, apoptosis, defective neuronal migration or oligodendrocyte maturation in affected human brain. Those candidate processes require separate evidence before entering a causal chain.

evidence.snippet: Congenital disorder of glycosylation type Ig (ALG12-CDG) is a rare inherited metabolic disease caused by a defect in alpha-mannosyltransferase 8, encoded by the ALG12 gene (22q13.33).
evidence.explanation: This directly identifies the disease-causing ALG12 enzyme defect.

evidence.snippet: The mechanism of pathogenicity is known to be loss-of-function.
evidence.explanation: ClinGen supports loss of ALG12 function as the curated mechanism.

evidence.snippet: In the patient's fibroblasts, the biosynthetic intermediate GlcNAc(2)Man(7) oligosaccharide was detected both on the lipid carrier dolichyl pyrophosphate and on newly synthesized glycoproteins, thus pointing to a defect in the dolichyl pyrophosphate-GlcNAc(2)Man(7)-dependent ALG12 alpha1,6 mannosyltransferase.
evidence.explanation: The original ALG12-CDG report directly localizes the ALG12 defect to dolichyl-pyrophosphate-linked oligosaccharide biosynthesis.

steps/1.description: Pathogenic ALG12 variants impair the alpha-mannosyltransferase step needed for dolichol-linked oligosaccharide biosynthesis and N-glycan precursor formation.

evidence.snippet: Due to a newborn Slovak patient's clinical and biochemical abnormalities, the isoelectric focusing of transferrin was performed with observed significant hypoglycosylation typical of CDG I.
evidence.explanation: The transferrin result directly supports a type I CDG hypoglycosylation pattern.

evidence.snippet: Intact serum transferrin showed, as expected for a CDG type I defect, underoccupancy of N-glycosylation sites.
evidence.explanation: This supports protein N-glycosylation underoccupancy as a downstream biochemical consequence.

steps/2.description: Impaired N-glycan precursor formation leads to hypoglycosylation of transferrin and other plasma proteins, consistent with a type I CDG biochemical pattern.

evidence.snippet: Currently reported features of ALG12-CDG include: developmental delay, hypotonia, failure to thrive and/or short stature, brain anomalies, recurrent infections, hypogammaglobulinemia, coagulation abnormalities, and genitourinary abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: The report summarizes the multisystem clinical spectrum downstream of ALG12-associated glycoprotein dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: ALG12-congenital disorder of glycosylation (ALG12-CDG) is a rare disorder caused by a deficiency of dolichol-P-mannose:Man7GlcNAc2-PP-dolichyl-α-6-mannosyltransferase which presents with intellectual disability, hypotonia, dysmorphic features, low IgG levels with recurrent infections, male genital hypoplasia, and coagulation abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: The case series links ALG12 deficiency to a multisystem phenotype without resolving the glycoprotein or tissue-specific intermediates.

steps/3.description: Defective N-glycosylation disrupts many glycoproteins and is associated with neurodevelopmental, growth, immune, coagulation, dysmorphic, and genitourinary manifestations. Rare severe prenatal renal-skeletal and exceptional adult cardioskeletal observations are modeled as separately bounded branches rather than core consequences.

evidence.snippet: Currently reported features of ALG12-CDG include: developmental delay, hypotonia, failure to thrive and/or short stature, brain anomalies, recurrent infections, hypogammaglobulinemia, coagulation abnormalities, and genitourinary abnormalities.

evidence.snippet: We here present an intriguing patient with an exceptional phenotype: 25-year-old women with a ventricular septal defect and severe idiopathic scoliosis but no facial dysmorphism, who dances as a professional, and has a University degree.

evidence.snippet: ALG12-CDG is a severe multisystem disease associated with low to deficient serum immunoglobulins and recurrent infections.
evidence.explanation: The glycophenotype report links ALG12-CDG to low serum immunoglobulins and recurrent infections.

evidence.snippet: As a whole, ALG12-CDG behaves as a dual CDG (CDG-I and II defects) and it is associated with distinct, abnormal glycosylation of total serum and IgG N-glycans.

steps/7.description: Abnormal total-serum and IgG N-glycan profiles co-occur with low immunoglobulins, recurrent infections, and hypoglycosylated coagulation proteins. The evidence does not establish a specific responsible cell type or a direct causal path to the immune findings.

evidence.snippet: The severe disease was identified in a child presenting with psychomotor retardation, hypotonia, growth retardation, dysmorphic features and anorexia.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report the finding of a novel missense mutation in the vesicle-associated membrane protein/synaptobrevin-associated membrane protein B (VAPB) gene in patients from this family.
evidence.explanation: The original identification of the causal VAPB variant.

evidence.snippet: A genetic mutation (P56S) in the conserved major sperm protein homology domain of VAPB has been linked to motor-neuron degeneration in affected amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) patients.
evidence.explanation: Locates the variant in the conserved MSP homology domain, which is what makes the FFAT-binding surface the affected function.

steps/1.description: A heterozygous germline missense change substitutes serine for a conserved proline at residue 56 of VAPB, within the N-terminal major sperm protein (MSP) homology domain — the surface through which VAPB binds FFAT-motif partners and so recruits lipid-transfer and other proteins to the cytosolic face of the endoplasmic reticulum. Essentially every reported family carries this one allele, inherited from a common founder.

evidence.snippet: We report that in the CNS, VAPB is abundant in motor neurons and that the P56S substitution causes aggregation of mutant VAPB in immobile tubular ER clusters, perturbs FFAT-motif binding, and traps endogenous VAP in mutant aggregates.
evidence.explanation: Documents both the aggregation itself and the sequestration of wild-type VAP that underlies the dominant-negative reading of the mechanism.

evidence.snippet: The data indicate that the VAPB-P56S inclusions represent a novel reversible ER quality control compartment that is formed when the amount of mutant VAPB exceeds the capacity of the ERAD pathway and that isolates misfolded and aggregated VAPB from the rest of the ER.
evidence.explanation: Characterizes the inclusions as an ERAD-linked quality-control compartment and, importantly, argues they may be protective rather than toxic — PARTIAL because it supports the existence of the node while qualifying its causal role.

evidence.snippet: The presence of these inclusions does not correlate with signs of axonal and neuronal degeneration, and axotomy leads to their gradual disappearance, indicating that they represent reversible structures.
evidence.explanation: Directly refutes a simple aggregate-causes-degeneration reading in the transgenic mouse: inclusion burden and degeneration are uncoupled.

steps/2.description: Mutant VAPB misfolds and self-associates into immobile, tubular ER-derived inclusions in motor neurons, dragging endogenous wild-type VAPA and VAPB into the same aggregates. The inclusions are not inert: they are decorated with ER-associated degradation machinery (p97/VCP, Derlin-1, BAP31) and behave as a quality-control compartment formed when misfolded VAPB exceeds ERAD capacity. Their pathogenic weight is contested — see the HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH discussion below, since patient-derived motor neurons expressing the allele at physiological level do not show them.

evidence.snippet: The mutant protein is aggregation-prone, non-functional and unstable, and its expression from a single allele appears to be insufficient to support toxic gain-of-function effects within motor neurons.
evidence.explanation: States the loss-of-function reading of the allele that this node represents.

evidence.snippet: We show for the first time that VAPB protein levels are reduced in ALS8-derived motor neurons but, in contrast to over-expression systems, cytoplasmic aggregates could not be identified.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates reduced VAPB in patient-derived motor neurons — the direct human-cell evidence for this node, and simultaneously the observation that the aggregate node is not seen at physiological expression.

evidence.snippet: Expression of VAPB mRNA and protein was predominantly localised to large motor neurones further supporting the relevance of this finding to disease progression occurring in SALS.
evidence.explanation: Localizes VAPB expression to large motor neurons in human spinal cord, which is why a VAPB shortfall is cell-type selective. Note this cohort is sporadic ALS, not VAPB-mutant disease.

evidence.snippet: One prominent function mediated by VAPB at these sites is lipid exchange, and a recurrent phenotype observed in all models investigating knockout or knockdown of VAPs is a significant increase in the levels of phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate (PI4P).
evidence.explanation: Names the lipid-exchange function lost and the PI4P readout that recurs across VAP-deficient models.

steps/3.description: However the aggregates are read, the functional consequence converges on too little working VAPB at the ER surface. The mutant protein is unstable and non-functional, and VAPB levels are reduced in patient-derived motor neurons and in ALS spinal cord. Because VAPB is the tether that recruits FFAT-motif partners to the ER, its shortfall degrades a whole family of contact-site functions at once: ER-to-Golgi transport, lipid exchange (with a characteristic rise in phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate), phosphoinositide and calcium handling, and ER protein quality control.

evidence.snippet: The mutant mice demonstrate induction of ER stress and autophagic response in motor neurons before obvious onset of behavioral defects, suggesting that these cellular biological defects might contribute to the initiation of the disease.
evidence.explanation: Places ER stress upstream of motor deficits at physiological expression levels.

evidence.snippet: Loss of Vap in flies shows various ERQC associated defects, including protein accumulation, ER expansion, and ER stress.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that losing VAP function is by itself sufficient to produce ER stress, linking this node to the loss-of-function arm rather than only to aggregation.

evidence.snippet: The P58S mutation in VAP33 leads to a failure to secrete the MSP domain as well as ubiquitination, accumulation of inclusions in the endoplasmic reticulum, and an unfolded protein response.
evidence.explanation: The Drosophila orthologue of the human variant produces ER inclusions and a UPR, and additionally fails to secrete the MSP domain — a distinct signalling loss noted here rather than curated as its own chain node because it is invertebrate-only evidence.

steps/4.description: Loss of VAPB-dependent ER quality control and accumulation of misfolded VAPB together activate the ER stress response in motor neurons. In physiological-level knock-in mice this is detectable before any behavioural deficit, which is what makes it a candidate initiating step rather than an end-stage epiphenomenon.

evidence.snippet: Finally, we demonstrate that VAPBP56S has altered binding to PTPIP51 and increases Ca(2+) uptake by mitochondria following release from ER stores.
evidence.explanation: Direct evidence that the disease allele changes the ER-mitochondria tether and its calcium function.

evidence.snippet: Here we show that the ER-resident protein VAPB interacts with the mitochondrial protein tyrosine phosphatase-interacting protein-51 (PTPIP51) to regulate ER-mitochondria associations.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the tethering function that the disease allele perturbs.

evidence.snippet: Inclusion formation was found to be a developmentally regulated process linked to mitochondrial damage that could be attenuated by reducing ER-mitochondrial contacts.
evidence.explanation: Reverses the expected direction of the arrow: mitochondrial damage feeds back on inclusion formation through the same contacts, so this node is part of a loop rather than a one-way step.

steps/5.description: VAPB is a mitochondria-associated-membrane protein that tethers ER to mitochondria by binding the outer-mitochondrial-membrane protein PTPIP51, and this contact is where calcium released from ER stores is taken up by mitochondria. p.Pro56Ser alters PTPIP51 binding and increases mitochondrial calcium uptake. PROVISIONAL rather than ESTABLISHED because the direct evidence comes from overexpression in cell lines and from yeast and mammalian model systems, not from VAPB-mutant human motor neurons.

evidence.snippet: Detailed investigations of autophagic flux in cell culture models revealed that P56S-VAPB alters both initial and late steps of the autophagy pathway.
evidence.explanation: Documents the autophagic-flux defect this node represents.

evidence.snippet: Autophagy and RBP homeostasis are interdependent, as demonstrated by the cytoplasmic mis-localisation of several RBPs including pTDP-43, FUS, Matrin 3 which often sequestered with P56S-VAPB aggregates both in cell culture and in the muscle biopsy of the ALS8 patient.
evidence.explanation: Links the autophagic defect to RNA-binding-protein mislocalization, including in human patient tissue.

steps/6.description: p.Pro56Ser disturbs both the initiation and the completion of autophagy, with autophagosomes failing to fuse with lysosomes. Aggregates accumulate together with LC3 and p62 and sequester RNA-binding proteins — phosphorylated TDP-43, FUS and Matrin 3 — into persistent stress granules, connecting this disorder to the wider TDP-43 proteinopathy of ALS. The human material is a single ALS8 index patient's muscle biopsy and fibroblasts, which is why the node is PROVISIONAL.

evidence.snippet: However, only a progressive loss of CSMNs but not SMNs was found in P56S VAPB Tg mice.
evidence.explanation: Supports motor neuron vulnerability while explicitly qualifying it: in this model the spinal motor neurons that define the human Finkel phenotype did not die.

evidence.snippet: In SMNs, P56S VAPB promoted a rather selective translocation of VAPB protein onto the postsynaptic site of C-boutons that altered the morphology of C-boutons and impaired the spontaneous rhythmic discharges of SMNs.
evidence.explanation: Gives the spinal motor neuron a dysfunction phenotype short of death, which is consistent with the very slow human course.

evidence.snippet: Significantly, the knock-in mice demonstrate accumulation of P56S VAPB protein and ubiquitinated proteins in cytoplasmic inclusions, selectively in motor neurons.
evidence.explanation: Establishes motor neuron selectivity of the cellular pathology at physiological expression level.

steps/7.description: Anterior-horn and brainstem lower motor neurons become dysfunctional and degenerate. Selectivity is striking and only partly explained: VAPB is abundant in motor neurons, and in the pan-neuronal transgenic mouse the corticospinal population is lost while spinal motor neurons instead show altered C-bouton morphology and impaired rhythmic discharge without frank loss. In humans the clinical picture at the Finkel end of the spectrum is purely lower motor neuron, whereas subtle pyramidal signs appear in a majority of ALS8 patients overall.

evidence.snippet: Electromyography disclosed ongoing denervation and reinnervation.
evidence.explanation: Direct human electrophysiological evidence for this node.

evidence.snippet: Electromyography showed widespread neuropathic damage.
evidence.explanation: Independent replication of the neurogenic electrodiagnostic pattern in an unrelated p.Pro56Ser family outside Brazil.

steps/8.description: Failing motor neurons denervate their muscle fibres; surviving units sprout and reinnervate them, which is why electromyography in these patients shows ongoing denervation together with reinnervation rather than acute denervation alone. This compensation is what buys the disorder its decades-long course, and its eventual exhaustion is what produces clinically apparent weakness.

evidence.snippet: Sural nerve biopsy revealed loss of nerve fibers, especially unmyelinated fibers.
evidence.explanation: The direct histological observation this node asserts.

evidence.snippet: This report indicates that VAPB-associated ALS may be accompanied by multifocal autonomic nerve damage.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own conclusion, and the hedge ("may be") that keeps this node at PROVISIONAL confidence.

evidence.snippet: Autonomic abnormalities were also present, including choking, chronic intestinal constipation, sexual dysfunction, and sudomotor abnormalities, and on nerve morphology there was involvement of unmyelinated fibers.
evidence.explanation: Independent replication of unmyelinated-fibre involvement, in the original Brazilian kindred rather than the Chinese family.

steps/9.description: A parallel, non-motor arm of the same VAPB deficit: peripheral autonomic and other unmyelinated fibres degenerate. Sural nerve biopsy in a p.Pro56Ser family showed loss of nerve fibres with a marked unmyelinated-fibre predominance and collagen pockets on electron microscopy, and the sympathetic skin response was absent. This is curated as a distinct arm rather than as part of lower motor neuron degeneration because the affected fibres are not motor, and as PROVISIONAL because it rests on two families — the original Brazilian kindred and an unrelated Chinese one — rather than on the large molecularly confirmed series, which did not assess autonomic function.

evidence.snippet: In this family, proximal and axial muscle weakness and atrophy, associated with abdominal protrusion, defined the motor phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Describes the motor endpoint of the chain in a VAPB p.Pro56Ser kindred.

evidence.snippet: Onset was lumbar in 94%, proximally predominant.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the proximal, lumbar-onset distribution across 78 molecularly confirmed patients.

steps/10.description: The clinical endpoint: proximal and axial weakness with neurogenic muscle atrophy, beginning in the lumbar region in the great majority of patients and ascending over years. Reflexes are reduced and sensation is preserved, which is what separates this from a sensorimotor neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: Median age at onset was 44.9 years; 51% were men.
evidence.explanation: Establishes adult onset with a median in the fifth decade and no sex bias.

evidence.snippet: Onset was lumbar in 94%, proximally predominant.
evidence.explanation: 94% of 78 molecularly confirmed patients had lumbar, proximally predominant onset, which maps to VERY_FREQUENT (80-100%).

evidence.snippet: In this family, proximal and axial muscle weakness and atrophy, associated with abdominal protrusion, defined the motor phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Independent family-level description of the proximal and axial distribution.

steps/11.description: The defining clinical feature. Weakness begins proximally, is lumbar in origin in the great majority of patients, and ascends over years. Axial involvement produces abdominal protrusion and, in some families, camptocormia.

evidence.snippet: In this family, proximal and axial muscle weakness and atrophy, associated with abdominal protrusion, defined the motor phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Documents atrophy alongside the weakness.

steps/12.description: Muscle wasting secondary to chronic denervation, accompanying the weakness in the same proximal and axial distribution.

evidence.snippet: The clinical features in all patients were camptocormia, fasciculation, and weakness in all limbs.
evidence.explanation: Documents fasciculation in every affected member of a p.Pro56Ser family.

steps/13.description: Visible spontaneous motor unit discharges, a cardinal sign of lower motor neuron disease and part of the reason this disorder enters the ALS differential.

evidence.snippet: The clinical features in all patients were camptocormia, fasciculation, and weakness in all limbs.
evidence.explanation: Documents camptocormia in all affected members of this family.

steps/14.description: Forward flexion of the trunk from axial (paraspinal) weakness. Reported as a uniform feature of the Chinese p.Pro56Ser kindred and the same axial involvement that produces abdominal protrusion in the Brazilian families.

evidence.snippet: Tone and tendon reflexes were decreased and a distal tremor was common.
evidence.explanation: Documents decreased tone and reflexes in the affected kindred.

steps/15.description: Hyporeflexia with reduced tone, the expected examination finding when the lesion is at the anterior horn cell and no upper motor neuron signs are present. Note that this is the Finkel-end finding; pyramidal signs are frequent across the wider ALS8 spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Tone and tendon reflexes were decreased and a distal tremor was common.
evidence.explanation: "Common" maps to FREQUENT (30-79%) under the GeneReviews prose-to-enum convention; no numerator was reported.

steps/16.description: A distal tremor, common in the affected kindred and a recognised accompaniment of chronic partial denervation with enlarged motor units. The deep-research artifact proposed postural tremor here; the cited source says only "distal tremor", so the generic HP:0001337 Tremor is retained rather than asserting a postural qualifier no cited abstract supports.

evidence.snippet: Autonomic abnormalities were also present, including choking, chronic intestinal constipation, sexual dysfunction, and sudomotor abnormalities, and on nerve morphology there was involvement of unmyelinated fibers.
evidence.explanation: Documents the autonomic syndrome and its unmyelinated-fibre substrate.

evidence.snippet: Two patients developed symptoms of dysautonomia, including abdominal bloating, orthostatic hypotension, constipation, frequent urination, decreased sweating, and burning feet.
evidence.explanation: Independent replication in an unrelated family, including the orthostatic hypotension this phenotype term names.

steps/17.description: Autonomic involvement — choking, constipation, sexual dysfunction, sudomotor abnormalities, orthostatic hypotension — with loss of unmyelinated fibres on nerve morphology. This is curated as a real but non-obligate feature of the p.Pro56Ser phenotype rather than as a defining one: the authors of the Brazilian kindred proposed that motor-plus-autonomic involvement constitutes a separate category of disease, and it was subsequently replicated in an unrelated Chinese family. It is not reported in most Finkel-type descriptions.

evidence.snippet: Autonomic abnormalities were also present, including choking, chronic intestinal constipation, sexual dysfunction, and sudomotor abnormalities, and on nerve morphology there was involvement of unmyelinated fibers.
evidence.explanation: Names chronic intestinal constipation among the autonomic features.

steps/18.description: Chronic intestinal constipation as part of the autonomic involvement.

evidence.snippet: Death occurred in 10-15 years due to respiratory insufficiency.
evidence.explanation: Identifies respiratory failure as the terminal event in this kindred.

evidence.snippet: Survival was 21.9 years; times to wheelchair dependence and noninvasive ventilation were 7.0 and 10.0 years, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the ventilation milestone across the largest reported series.

steps/19.description: Respiratory muscle involvement is the principal cause of death and the milestone that most shapes management. Median time from onset to noninvasive ventilation is 10 years across the ALS8 series; in the dysautonomic Brazilian kindred death occurred in 10-15 years from respiratory insufficiency.

evidence.snippet: Bulbar involvement occurred in 17 (21.8%) patients, predominantly as dysphonia.
evidence.explanation: 21.8% maps to OCCASIONAL (5-29%), and the paper names dysphonia as the predominant form.

evidence.snippet: A rare, genetic, motor neuron disease characterized by adulthood-onset of slowly progressive, proximal muscular weakness with fasciculations, amyotrophy, cramps, and absent/hypoactive reflexes, without bulbar or pyramidal involvement.
evidence.explanation: Orphanet's definition of this entity excludes bulbar involvement, which the 21.8% figure from the molecularly confirmed series contradicts. Curated as REFUTE for the same reason as the pyramidal-signs node: the disagreement is between a nosological definition and a genotype-defined cohort, and is the substance of this entry's scope problem.

steps/20.description: Bulbar features occur in about a fifth of ALS8 patients and are predominantly dysphonia rather than the dysarthria-dysphagia pattern of bulbar-onset ALS. Not an early or defining feature of the Finkel-type presentation.

evidence.snippet: Survival was 21.9 years; times to wheelchair dependence and noninvasive ventilation were 7.0 and 10.0 years, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Gives the median time to wheelchair dependence.

steps/21.description: Wheelchair dependence is reached at a median of 7 years from onset — early relative to the 21.9-year median survival, so most patients live many years with substantial motor disability rather than dying soon after losing ambulation.

edges/8.description: VAPB is not motor-neuron-specific, so the same functional shortfall is the presumed cause of the autonomic and small-fibre arm. The intermediates are unknown: nothing in this literature explains why some carriers develop dysautonomia and most do not, and no cell-type-selective mechanism has been proposed.

edges/13.description: Loss of the efferent limb of the monosynaptic stretch reflex. This is why reflexes are reduced or absent rather than brisk, and it is the sign that keeps the bedside picture in the lower motor neuron column.

edges/14.description: Extension of the same anterior-horn process to brainstem lower motor neurons. Because it is the bulbar motor nucleus rather than the corticobulbar tract that fails, the resulting deficit is predominantly dysphonia rather than the spastic dysarthria of bulbar-onset ALS.

evidence.snippet: The clinical features in all patients were camptocormia, fasciculation, and weakness in all limbs.
evidence.explanation: Reports fasciculation alongside the widespread neuropathic EMG damage that defines this node, in the same patients.

edges/16.description: Spontaneous discharge of unstable, partly denervated motor units — the clinical surface of the denervation-reinnervation process this node describes.

edges/17.description: Muscle fibres that lose their motor neuron and are not recaptured by a sprouting neighbour atrophy, giving the grouped-fibre pattern of a neurogenic rather than myopathic process.

edges/18.description: Postural tremor attributed to the enlarged motor units produced by collateral reinnervation, not to a cerebellar or extrapyramidal lesion. Curated as an indirect edge because the intermediate is inferred from general motor-unit physiology rather than measured in these patients.

edges/19.description: The clinical expression of this node: proximal, lumbar-predominant weakness that ascends over years.

evidence.snippet: The clinical features in all patients were camptocormia, fasciculation, and weakness in all limbs.
evidence.explanation: Places camptocormia alongside limb weakness as an expression of the same neurogenic process in a p.Pro56Ser family.

edges/20.description: Axial extension of the same neurogenic weakness. Failure of the paraspinal extensors produces forward flexion of the trunk, and of the abdominal wall the abdominal protrusion described in the original kindred.

edges/21.description: Wheelchair dependence at a median of 7 years from onset is the point at which the accumulating proximal deficit crosses a functional threshold, not a separate mechanism.

edges/22.description: The same ascending neurogenic weakness reaching the respiratory muscles, which is why noninvasive ventilation follows loss of ambulation on a predictable interval (7 years to wheelchair, 10 to ventilation) and why respiratory failure is the terminal event.

edges/23.description: Loss of peripheral autonomic fibres produces the sudomotor, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal and sexual dysfunction recorded as the dysautonomia phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Two patients developed symptoms of dysautonomia, including abdominal bloating, orthostatic hypotension, constipation, frequent urination, decreased sweating, and burning feet.
evidence.explanation: Lists constipation as a component of the dysautonomia syndrome, which is the claim this edge makes.

edges/24.description: Constipation is curated as its own phenotype because it is the autonomic feature patients report most, but mechanistically it is one manifestation of the dysautonomia node rather than an independent process.

evidence.snippet: Subsequently, the same mutation was identified in patients from six additional kindreds but with different clinical courses, such as ALS8, late-onset SMA, and typical severe ALS with rapid progression.
evidence.explanation: Establishes gene-disease causation and, in the same sentence, the one-allele-many-phenotypes problem.

evidence.snippet: Eight families, comprising more than 1,500 individuals of whom about 200 are affected, are now known to carry this mutation.
evidence.explanation: Gives the size of the known p.Pro56Ser population and its family structure.

evidence.snippet: The VAP proteins are integral adaptor proteins of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane that recruit a myriad of interacting partners to the ER surface.
evidence.explanation: States the normal molecular function of the affected protein.

evidence.snippet: In order to identify additional ALS-associated VAPB mutations, we screened the entire VAPB gene in a cohort of ALS patients and detected two mutations (A145V and S160Δ).
evidence.explanation: Documents the additional VAPB alleles found in ALS cohorts, which are not the Finkel-type allele.

genes/0.notes:
VAPB (20q13.32) encodes VAMP-associated protein B/C, a type II integral membrane protein of the endoplasmic reticulum whose cytosolic MSP domain recruits FFAT-motif partners and so builds membrane contact sites between the ER and essentially every other cellular membrane. The recurrent disease allele is c.166C>T (p.Pro56Ser), which lies in the MSP domain.
Two facts about this gene shape how a VAPB result should be read. First, p.Pro56Ser is not a set of independent observations: haplotype analysis of eight families of both Portuguese-Brazilian and African-Brazilian ancestry traces them all to one founding event about 23 generations ago, so the apparent recurrence of the allele is largely genealogy. Second, one allele does not equal one phenotype — the same p.Pro56Ser produces late-onset SMA, slowly progressive atypical ALS, and rapidly progressive typical ALS in different kindreds, and no modifier explaining that has been identified.
Other VAPB variants (T46I, A145V, S160del) have been reported in ALS cohorts, but the Finkel-type SMA phenotype curated here is a p.Pro56Ser phenotype; nothing establishes that the other alleles produce it.

evidence.snippet: Survival was 21.9 years; times to wheelchair dependence and noninvasive ventilation were 7.0 and 10.0 years, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Establishes noninvasive ventilation as a milestone actually reached by this p.Pro56Ser cohort, and dates it, which is what makes it curatable here rather than merely plausible by analogy with ALS.

evidence.snippet: Non-invasive ventilation (NIV), which is the main recognized treatment for alleviating the symptoms of respiratory failure, prolongs survival and improves quality of life.
evidence.explanation: Expert-panel respiratory-care guidance for motor neurone disease naming NIV as the main recognized treatment for the respiratory failure this disorder ends in. PARTIAL, not SUPPORT, on the same ground as the Bourke trial below: the guidance is written for ALS, not for VAPB p.Pro56Ser carriers. ALS8 sits inside that clinical category and 51% of the p.Pro56Ser series presented as spinal-onset ALS, but that is an extrapolation and is tagged as one.

evidence.snippet: This subgroup showed improvement in several measures of quality of life and a median survival benefit of 205 days (p=0.006) with maintained quality of life for most of this period.
evidence.explanation: The controlled evidence that NIV extends survival and preserves quality of life in motor neurone disease. Marked PARTIAL rather than SUPPORT because the trial was in ALS, not in VAPB p.Pro56Ser carriers, and its benefit was confined to the subgroup with better bulbar function — no NIV trial has been run in this disorder, and none is likely at this prevalence.

treatments/0.description: Ventilatory support, typically bilevel positive airway pressure, once respiratory muscle weakness produces orthostatic breathlessness, orthopnoea or nocturnal hypoventilation. This is the single most consequential supportive intervention in this disorder because respiratory insufficiency is the terminal event, and because the natural history is slow and predictable enough to anticipate: the molecularly confirmed p.Pro56Ser series places the median time from onset to noninvasive ventilation at 10 years, three years after wheelchair dependence. It is not disease-modifying — see the vapb_no_disease_modifying_therapy discussion — and it does not slow denervation.

evidence.snippet: Survival was 21.9 years; times to wheelchair dependence and noninvasive ventilation were 7.0 and 10.0 years, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Ties the intervention to this disorder's respiratory endpoint on a dated milestone rather than a general indication.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: NIV supplies mechanically the inspiratory pressure that denervated diaphragmatic and intercostal motor units can no longer generate. It works around the failing effector rather than acting anywhere on the upstream VAPB chain, which is why the effect is BYPASSES and why it is compatible with continued progression of the mechanism it compensates for.

evidence.snippet: This review will present rehabilitation strategies that can be utilized to maximize patient independence, function, safety, and quality of life, and to minimize disease-related symptoms.
evidence.explanation: States the goal and scope of rehabilitation in progressive motor neurone disease. PARTIAL because it is a narrative review addressed to ALS, with no VAPB-specific rehabilitation study to cite; the stage-matched principle transfers, the effect size is not established for this disorder.

evidence.snippet: Survival was 21.9 years; times to wheelchair dependence and noninvasive ventilation were 7.0 and 10.0 years, respectively.
evidence.explanation: The gap between wheelchair dependence at 7 years and death at 21.9 is the disease-specific reason rehabilitation matters here — it quantifies the long period of survival with disability that rehabilitation is addressed to.

treatments/1.description: Stage-matched rehabilitation — range-of-motion work, gait and transfer training, orthoses, mobility aids and eventually wheelchair provision — aimed at independence, safety and prevention of secondary complications such as contractures and falls. The unusually long course here makes this weigh more than it does in typical ALS: median survival is 21.9 years while wheelchair dependence arrives at 7, so most patients live over a decade with substantial motor disability.

evidence.snippet: Given the progressive nature of ALS, the clinician must be aware of the expected disease trajectory and apply appropriate interventions at each stage.
evidence.explanation: The stage-matched principle that connects the intervention to the ambulation milestone. PARTIAL for the same ALS-versus-ALS8 reason as above.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Rehabilitation acts on the functional consequence, not on the denervation producing it: gait training, orthoses and mobility aids alter how much disability a given degree of proximal weakness imposes and when the wheelchair threshold is crossed. MODULATES rather than INHIBITS because no evidence shows rehabilitation slows motor unit loss.

evidence.snippet: These findings expand the phenotypic characterization of ALS8 and support genetic counseling and anticipatory management.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own statement of what the natural-history data are for. No target_mechanisms is set because counselling is a non-therapeutic action and does not act on a pathograph node.

treatments/2.description: Counselling for an autosomal dominant, adult-onset, fully penetrant-appearing founder allele, where at-risk relatives are typically adults who have already reproduced. The 78-patient natural-history series explicitly frames its own findings as supporting genetic counselling and anticipatory management, which is the practical output of characterizing a course this predictable.

evidence.snippet: Our data support a model in which reduced levels of VAP family proteins result in decreased ER anchoring of lipid-binding proteins and cause motor neuron degeneration.
evidence.explanation: States the sequestration model in the authors' own terms.

hypotheses/0.description: The historically dominant reading: mutant VAPB misfolds, forms ER-derived aggregates, and recruits the wild-type VAPA and VAPB products of the normal alleles into those aggregates, so that a heterozygote loses far more VAP function than the 50% a null allele would cost. This explains dominance without invoking a novel toxic activity, and it is directly demonstrated — but in overexpression systems.

evidence.snippet: Instead, loss-of-function of the single wild-type allele is required for pathological effects, and VAPB haploinsufficiency may be the main driver of the disease.
evidence.explanation: States the haploinsufficiency hypothesis explicitly.

evidence.snippet: Thus, Vapb loss of function weakens the motor system of vertebrate animal models but is on its own unable to lead to a complete ALS phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Supports a loss-of-function contribution while showing it is not sufficient on its own — which is why this hypothesis is EMERGING rather than superseding the dominant-negative account.

hypotheses/1.description: The competing reading: at physiological expression a single mutant allele produces too little protein to sequester anything, aggregates are not seen in patient-derived cells, and what actually matters is that the wild-type allele alone cannot supply enough VAPB. On this account the disorder is a haploinsufficiency and the aggregates seen in overexpression systems are an artefact of dose. The two hypotheses are not mutually exclusive — both converge on the same central_effector node — but they imply opposite therapeutic strategies (clear the aggregate versus raise wild-type VAPB).

evidence.snippet: At admission, 51% had spinal-onset ALS, 42% progressive muscular atrophy (PMA) and 6% flail leg; 30% of patients with PMA subsequently developed UMN signs.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the phenotypic split within one allele and the partial conversion between categories over time.

evidence.snippet: A rare, genetic, motor neuron disease characterized by adulthood-onset of slowly progressive, proximal muscular weakness with fasciculations, amyotrophy, cramps, and absent/hypoactive reflexes, without bulbar or pyramidal involvement.
evidence.explanation: Supplies the other half of the problem. Orphanet keeps this entity distinct from ALS8 by defining it as free of bulbar and pyramidal involvement, but the allele that causes it produces both in most carriers. The gap between the reference nosology and the molecular cohort is what makes it unclear whether MONDO:0008453 names a disease or a presentation.

evidence.snippet: Over the past 68 years, the Finkel type late-onset adult autosomal dominant spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) that is allelic with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-8 (ALS8) gained a genotype-phenotype correlation among the motor neuron diseases through the work of groups led by Zatz and Marques Jr.
evidence.explanation: States the allelism directly: Finkel-type SMA and ALS8 are the same locus, which is the premise of this discussion. The open question is not whether the two labels share an allele but why the shared allele produces both. Tagged OTHER because it is a historical review, not a study contributing observations.

open_questions/0.rationale: This is the central unresolved question for this entry, and it is unusually well posed because the founder effect removes allelic heterogeneity as an explanation: nearly all reported patients carry the same ancestral chromosome. The 2004 discovery paper already reported the three courses across seven kindreds, and the 2026 series of 78 patients quantified the split — 42% presenting as pure progressive muscular atrophy, of whom 30% later developed upper motor neuron signs. Whatever separates them is therefore modifier, environmental or stochastic, and none has been identified. Practically, this determines whether MONDO:0008453 names a disease or a presentation.

evidence.snippet: Our results suggest that optimal levels of VAPB may play a central role in the pathogenesis of ALS8, in agreement with the observed reduction of VAPB in sporadic ALS.
evidence.explanation: The patient-cell result reframing the mechanism around VAPB levels rather than aggregates.

evidence.snippet: The presence of these inclusions does not correlate with signs of axonal and neuronal degeneration, and axotomy leads to their gradual disappearance, indicating that they represent reversible structures.
evidence.explanation: Uncouples inclusion burden from degeneration in the model where the inclusions are most conspicuous.

open_questions/1.rationale: The aggregation-and-sequestration model was built almost entirely in overexpression systems, where mutant VAPB reliably forms tubular ER clusters and drags in wild-type VAP. Three lines of evidence complicate transferring that to patients. Patient-derived iPSC motor neurons show reduced VAPB but no identifiable cytoplasmic aggregates. In transgenic mice the inclusions do not correlate with degeneration, disappear after axotomy, and behave as a reversible ERAD-linked quality-control compartment — possibly protective. Against that, physiological-level knock-in mice do form motor-neuron inclusions, so dose alone does not explain the discrepancy. The mismatch is not academic: it decides whether a therapy should clear aggregates or restore wild-type VAPB, and the two hypotheses in mechanistic_hypotheses point in opposite directions.

open_questions/2.rationale: Every treatment curated in this entry is supportive: rehabilitation, mobility aids, noninvasive ventilation, genetic counselling. None of it is disease-modifying, and nothing in `treatments` should be read as implying otherwise — the `target_mechanisms` links land on the downstream manifestations (`Respiratory Insufficiency`, `Loss of Ambulation`) and nowhere on the VAPB chain that produces them. Nutritional and swallowing support belong in the same category but are not curated for want of a disorder-specific citation. The specific hazard worth naming is the shared "spinal muscular atrophy" label: nusinersen, risdiplam and onasemnogene abeparvovec raise SMN protein and are approved for SMN1-related 5q SMA. VAPB disease is non-5q and has normal SMN; those agents have no mechanistic route to it and must not be curated here as treatments. The 21.9-year median survival and the 7-year and 10-year milestones to wheelchair and ventilation are, at present, the substance of what can be offered: anticipatory management on a predictable timeline.

evidence.snippet: Twinning was confirmed as a risk factor for both ABS and LBWC.
evidence.explanation: The large EUROCAT analysis supports twinning as a risk factor.

evidence.snippet: We found a significantly higher rate of prior uterine surgeries (p = 0.008) in patient with ABS compared to control.
evidence.explanation: The ten-pregnancy study supports an association but is too small for a universal claim.

evidence.snippet: Amniotic rupture appeared to cause injury through three basic mechanisms
evidence.explanation: The human series supports rupture as an initiating event in this model.

evidence.snippet: Amniotic rupture sequence (ARS) is a disruption sequence presenting with fibrous bands, possibly emerging as a result of amniotic tear in the first trimester of gestation.
evidence.explanation: The registry paper explicitly qualifies the rupture origin as possible.

steps/2.description: Rupture or separation of the amnion is the proposed initiating event in the extrinsic model. It is provisional because rupture is not demonstrated in every case and ABS remains etiologically heterogeneous.

evidence.snippet: may be associated with fetalplacental fibrous bands.
evidence.explanation: The review supports fibrous bands as an association rather than an invariant.

steps/3.description: Fibrous strands in the amniotic cavity are the physical substrate of the extrinsic band-positive model. Their formation or exposure is provisional because fetal-placental bands are associated with, rather than present in, every clinically labeled case.

evidence.snippet: Most of the craniofacial defects (encephaloceles and/or facial clefts) occurring in these fetuses are not caused by constrictive amniotic bands, but are the result of a vascular disruption sequence with or without cephalo-amniotic adhesion.
evidence.explanation: Fetopathology supports a distinct vascular/adhesion route for these lesions.

steps/4.description: Fetopathologic observations propose a vascular disruption sequence for many encephaloceles and facial clefts occurring in fetuses with amniotic bands, with or without a broad cephalo-amniotic adhesion. This alternative is not treated as a downstream consequence of limb-band compression.

evidence.snippet: the clinical consequences result from fetal parts becoming entangled in the amnion.
evidence.explanation: This review directly supports fetal-part entanglement.

steps/5.description: A limb, digit, craniofacial structure, or umbilical cord may become caught by a strand. The resulting focal tether transmits abnormal mechanical force and can progress to circumferential compression.

evidence.snippet: Compression from the rings may lead to edema, skeletal anomalies (e.g. fractures, foot deformities) and, infrequently, neural compromise.
evidence.explanation: Orphanet directly links ring compression to tissue sequelae.

evidence.snippet: Of these 36 foetuses, limb constriction rings were produced in 35 (97%), and an in utero limb amputation in one (3%).
evidence.explanation: The ligature model demonstrates rings and rare amputation after compression.

steps/6.description: Circumferential band pressure creates the defining ring indentation and can obstruct distal fluid drainage, blood flow, or nerve integrity. This node represents mechanical compression, not a universal cause for band-negative cases.

evidence.snippet: Compression from the rings may lead to edema
evidence.explanation: This supports distal fluid accumulation without resolving vessel-level detail.

steps/7.description: Compression that preferentially impairs venous and lymphatic return causes swelling distal to a ring. The specific drainage sequence is clinically plausible but not directly measured in the available ABS series.

evidence.snippet: recovery of the involved distal limb perfusion
evidence.explanation: Recovery after band release supports distal perfusion compromise.

evidence.snippet: The ligated limbs showed an amputation or quasiamputation. Four extremities showed a necrotic pattern and 4 an edema pattern.
evidence.explanation: Controlled fetal-lamb ligation supports edema, necrosis, and tissue loss after compression.

steps/8.description: More severe or persistent constriction can reduce distal perfusion. Reversibility after fetoscopic release and edema/necrosis after experimental fetal-limb ligation support compression as the proximal lesion.

evidence.snippet: Compression from the rings may lead to edema, skeletal anomalies (e.g. fractures, foot deformities) and, infrequently, neural compromise.
evidence.explanation: Orphanet directly supports infrequent neural compromise from ring compression.

steps/9.description: Deep constriction rings can compromise local nerves. This is kept separate from perfusion failure because the available structured evidence establishes only that neural compromise can occur, not its frequency or relationship to tissue ischemia.

evidence.snippet: minor and distal limb defects (phalangeal or digital amputation, pseudosyndactyly, constriction rings) predominated in the ARS-L group
evidence.explanation: Registry data document distal amputations in limb-predominant cases.

evidence.snippet: One of these four did not have the band released and underwent fetal demise at 24 weeks.
evidence.explanation: The small series documents severe outcome with unreleased cord involvement.

evidence.snippet: These abnormalities included: (1) upper limb defects: syndactyly, amputation at the level of phalanges or first metacarpal or forearm;
evidence.explanation: Prenatal cases document upper-limb deformation and loss patterns.

steps/12.description: Tethering, crowding, and altered movement can deform limb position or relationships without requiring complete vascular interruption. This branch covers talipes, contracture, scoliosis, and syndactyly-like presentations.

evidence.snippet: Its agent is a spotted fever group rickettsia, member of the Rickettsia conorii complex, transmitted to humans by Rhipicephalus sanguineus and Rhipicephalus pumilio ticks.
evidence.explanation: The molecular survey states that the Astrakhan fever agent is transmitted to humans by Rhipicephalus ticks, supporting tick-mediated inoculation as the initiating exposure.

steps/0.description: An infected R. pumilio or R. sanguineus tick bites human skin and delivers R. conorii subsp. caspia into the dermis, seeding the local and systemic spotted-fever-group infection.

evidence.snippet: The unique lifestyle features of rickettsiae include obligate intracellular parasitism, intracytoplasmic niche within the host cell, predilection for infection of microvascular endothelium in mammalian hosts, association with arthropods and the tendency for genomic reduction.
evidence.explanation: The rickettsial review establishes the shared cytosolic and endothelial tropism inferred for the Astrakhan fever agent.

steps/1.description: Rickettsia species replicate inside host cells, especially mammalian microvascular endothelial cells; this shared cytosolic niche is inferred for R. conorii subsp. caspia from its membership in the spotted-fever Rickettsia lineage.

evidence.snippet: Clinicomorphological characteristics are given of primary reaction at the site of tick (Rhipicephalus pumilio) bite in new rickettsiosis spreading in Astrakhan Province--Astrakhan fever.
evidence.explanation: The Astrakhan fever clinical-morphologic report centers the primary bite-site reaction after R. pumilio exposure.

steps/2.description: R. conorii subsp. caspia infection after an R. pumilio bite produces a primary reaction at the inoculation site, with regional lymph-node drainage before or alongside disseminated Astrakhan fever.

evidence.snippet: The disease presented with long-term fever (body temperature 39-40 degrees C), intoxication, conjunctivitis, hepatomegaly, regional lymphadenitis, disseminated roseolous papular-hemorrhagic rash, arterial hypotension.
evidence.explanation: The primary-lesion report ties Astrakhan fever to a disseminated inflammatory clinical syndrome after an R. pumilio bite-site reaction.

evidence.snippet: Comparative study of interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor production under conditions of experimental rickettsial infection caused by agents of Astrakhan spotted fever and North Asian scrub typhus showed that therapy with galavit reduced manifestations of the disease, decreased mortality of experimental animals, and decreased the concentrations of interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor to normal values.
evidence.explanation: Experimental Astrakhan fever infection engaged the inflammatory cytokines IL-1 and TNF in an animal model.

steps/3.description: Local and disseminated rickettsial infection inflames small cutaneous and systemic vessels, producing the fever, conjunctival, lymph-node, hepatic, rash, and hemodynamic manifestations reported in Astrakhan fever.

evidence.snippet: Examination of immunocompetent cells has revealed suppression of T- and B-immunity for 2 weeks in moderate AF and 3 weeks in severe AF.
evidence.explanation: The 75-patient cellular-immunity study reports a transient Astrakhan fever-associated suppression of T- and B-cell compartments.

steps/4.description: Moderate Astrakhan fever suppresses measured T- and B-cell immunity for about two weeks, while severe disease prolongs that suppression to about three weeks.

evidence.snippet: This defect can be due to a lesion or defect in the inner hair cell (IHC), IHC ribbon synapse (e.g., pre-synaptic release of glutamate), postsynaptic terminals of the spiral ganglion neurons, or demyelination and axonal loss within the auditory nerve.

evidence.snippet: We found otoferlin to be required for proper synapse development in the immature rodent cochlea: In absence of otoferlin, synaptic pruning was delayed, and postsynaptic boutons appeared enlarged at 2 weeks of age.

evidence.snippet: A novel nonsense mutation (p.Y1064X) and a known pathogenic mutation (p.R1939Q) of the OTOF gene were identified in a patient as compound heterozygote.

evidence.snippet: Abnormal discharge of auditory fibers results from lesions involving the nerve fibers themselves (postsynaptic AN), the inner hair cells (IHCs) or their synapses with auditory nerve terminals (presynaptic AN) [1].

evidence.snippet: The demyelination of auditory nerve fibers observed in demyelinating neuropathies is expected to result in slowed conduction velocity with consequent disruption of temporal coding of acoustic signals (desynchrony)
evidence.explanation: Links auditory nerve demyelination to temporal dyssynchrony.

steps/9.description: Postsynaptic ANSD involves spiral ganglion terminals or auditory nerve fibers; impaired spike initiation, demyelination, axonal loss, or distal dendritic dysfunction reduce temporal precision of auditory nerve discharge.

evidence.snippet: On the one hand, the mitochondrial import of ETC complex subunits was inhibited, subsequently leading to an increased ADP/ATP ratio and elevated ROS levels.

evidence.snippet: Auditory neuropathy (AN) is a unique type of language developmental disorder, with no precise rate of genetic contribution that has been deciphered in a large cohort.
evidence.explanation: Supports auditory neuropathy as a hearing-related developmental disorder evaluated in a large human cohort.

evidence.snippet: Auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder (ANSD) refers to a range of hearing impairments characterized by an impaired transmission of sound from the cochlea to the brain.
evidence.explanation: Defines ANSD as a hearing-impairment spectrum.

steps/12.description: Hearing thresholds are variable, ranging from mild to profound impairment, and may improve, remain stable, fluctuate, or deteriorate depending on etiology and lesion site.

evidence.snippet: The disruption of auditory nerve discharge underlies both the absence of or profound alterations in auditory brainstem responses and the severe impairment of speech perception.

evidence.snippet: some patients with AN may have normal hearing thresholds and an impairment of speech perception that is only apparent in the presence of noise
evidence.explanation: Supports speech-in-noise impairment as an important clinical feature that may be missed by threshold testing.

steps/13.description: Speech perception is often disproportionately poor relative to pure-tone thresholds because temporal neural coding is impaired.

evidence.snippet: Auditory neuropathy is a rare form of deafness characterized by an absent or abnormal auditory brainstem response with preservation of outer hair cell function.
evidence.explanation: Provides the classic ABR/OHC diagnostic contrast.

evidence.snippet: Its diagnosis is based on presence of otoacoustic emissions and lack of, or abnormal, brainstem auditory evoked potential.

steps/14.description: Absent auditory brainstem responses are a core ANSD finding. Markedly abnormal responses also satisfy the broader diagnostic pattern but are not asserted through this absence-specific HPO binding.

evidence.snippet: Auditory neuropathy is a rare form of deafness characterized by an absent or abnormal auditory brainstem response with preservation of outer hair cell function.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the electrophysiologic consequence represented by this edge.

evidence.explanation: Supports impaired otoferlin-dependent vesicle replenishment as the presynaptic lesion underlying unreliable auditory coding.

edges/10.description: Temporal coding impairment causes speech perception to be reduced out of proportion to hearing threshold elevation.

evidence.snippet: Mitochondrial dysfunction, especially mCa2+ overload, plays a prominent role in ANSD associated with AIFM1.

edges/11.description: In AIFM1-associated ANSD, mitochondrial calcium overload and energetic injury in patient-derived neurons contribute to the auditory phenotype.

evidence.snippet: These mutations could result in developmental defects in GLSs and a diminished capacity for gap junction function, which may be implicated in the auditory deficits observed in ANSD patients.

edges/12.description: Impaired cochlear support-cell gap-junction communication is implicated in the auditory deficits of TMEM43-associated ANSD.

evidence.explanation: Establishes DIAPH3 as the causative gene for autosomal dominant nonsyndromic auditory neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: DIAPH3 | HGNC:15480 | auditory neuropathy | MONDO:0021944 | AD | Limited
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies the DIAPH3-auditory neuropathy gene-disease relationship as limited with autosomal dominant inheritance.

genes/0.notes: DIAPH3 overexpression causes AUNA1, an autosomal dominant nonsyndromic auditory neuropathy subtype.

evidence.explanation: Directly supports cochlear implantation while noting cochlear nerve deficiency as an outcome modifier.

treatments/1.description: Cochlear implantation is a major rehabilitative option for selected ANSD patients, with outcomes influenced by lesion site and cochlear nerve integrity.

evidence.snippet: the US Food and Drug Administration announced on April 23rd the approval of Otarmeni, the first gene therapy for a genetic form of hearing loss
evidence.explanation: The 2026 editorial records the FDA approval and its gene-specific scope.

evidence.snippet: DB-OTO gene therapy improved hearing in patients with OTOF-related deafness, enabling natural acoustic hearing and normalizing hearing sensitivity in 3 of 12 treated patients.
evidence.explanation: First-in-human registrational study supports clinically meaningful hearing restoration.

treatments/2.description: Intracochlear dual-AAV1 OTOF gene replacement is an FDA-approved, gene-specific option in the United States for eligible OTOF-related severe to profound hearing loss. evidence.explanation: Multicentre single-arm data support efficacy across a broad age range and follow-up to 2.5 years.

evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports early identification as a prerequisite for language-focused habilitation; ANSD-specific modality selection still depends on lesion site and response.

evidence.snippet: In 8 Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT) families we identified 4 pathogenic heterozygous GDAP1 mutations, 3 of which are novel. Three of the mutations displayed reduced disease penetrance. Disease onset in the affected individuals was variable, ranging from early childhood to adulthood. Disease progression was slow in most patients and overall severity milder than typically seen in autosomal recessive GDAP1 mutations.
evidence.explanation: Eight ascertained families establish dominant inheritance and variable expression; seven families were recruited separately from the 97-family screening cohort.

steps/1.description: A dominant pathogenic GDAP1 allele perturbs peripheral nerve function. The experimentally measured consequences depend on the allele, construct and cell system; this node does not imply loss of the wild-type allele or a proven universal dominant-negative interaction.

evidence.snippet: The apparent Tm value for wtGDAP1, ~62°C, was >5°C higher than for both mutants, suggesting that the effect of the mutations may be linked to an overall destabilization of the fold.
evidence.explanation: R120W/H123R soluble fragments were tested by apparent melting temperature; this is not a cellular protein-turnover assay.

evidence.snippet: For the mutations at position 310, it was observed that both R310Q and R310W in fact increased the stability of GDAP1Δ319–358 by ~1°C
evidence.explanation: The longer soluble R310 constructs provide an exception to universal destabilization.

steps/2.description: Purified soluble R120W and H123R GDAP1 fragments retain a broadly similar fold but have lower apparent thermal stability. The transmembrane anchor is absent from these constructs. This is an allele-scoped molecular readout, without a demonstrated causal bridge to fusion or neuronal loss. Other tested substitutions, including R310Q/W, need not destabilize the protein.

evidence.snippet: CI enzymatic activity was about 50% lower in the p. C240Y fibroblasts compared to controls (Fig. 1a, p=0.01), while only reduced by 30% in the p.R120W fi broblasts (Fig. 1a, p=0.09).
evidence.explanation: The enzyme-activity reduction was significant for C240Y but not R120W in two-family fibroblast comparisons.

Complex I subunit abundance and blue-native assembly were preserved. This is not evidence that all dominant GDAP1 alleles directly inhibit the respiratory complex.

evidence.snippet: Measurements of mitochondrial oxygen consumption re vealed that using CI malate-pyruvate (MP) substrates, the respiratory rate (Fig. 1b) and the corresponding ATP production (Fig. 1c) were significantly lower in both mutant cell lines, compared to controls (40%, p<0.05 in both measurements).
evidence.explanation: Permeabilized fibroblasts from both families had lower complex-I-substrate respiration and ATP synthesis under the experimental conditions.

steps/4.description: Complex-I-substrate-driven ATP synthesis is reduced in permeabilized C240Y and R120W fibroblasts. This substrate-specific flux measurement does not establish universal cellular ATP depletion or bioenergetic failure in dominant CMT2K neurons.

evidence.snippet: Conversely, the fusion process was dramatically impaired in cells expressing the Ala156Gly variant or the known dominant Arg120Trp GDAP1 mutation (figure 3).
evidence.explanation: A156G and R120W were assessed in transfected cell fusion assays, not patient axons.

steps/5.description: A156G and R120W expression impairs mitochondrial fusion in cell-based assays. The earlier experimental panel also distinguishes dominant fusion interference from reduced fission with recessive variants. This distinction is supported for tested variants, not every GDAP1 genotype.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, impaired fusion process resulted in fragmented mitochondria in cells expressing the Ala156Gly mutant (figure e-1A on the Neurology® Web site at www.neurology.org) and increased sensitivity to proapoptotic agents, as quantified by a cytochrome c release assay, which was also in line with our previous findings for other dominant GDAP1 mutations (figure e-1, B and C).15
evidence.explanation: Mitochondrial fragmentation and stimulus-dependent cytochrome-c release were measured in the A156G expression system.

steps/6.description: Cells expressing the dominant A156G variant show fragmented mitochondrial networks. Static morphology and fusion assays are related but distinct readouts; fragmentation is not established as a universal finding in patient-derived fibroblasts.

evidence.snippet: Using a fluorescent probe specific for superoxide a nions (MitoSOX TM ), we identified a 40% enhancement of fluorescence intensity in p.C240Y fi broblasts compared to controls (Fig. 4a and 4b, p=0.020). In addition, we observed a 50% decrease in thiol group level, which are the ROS targets, further supporting ROS overproduction (Fig. 4c, p=0.015). Moreover, the expression of manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), a major mitochondrial antioxidant, was 53% higher in p.C240Y fibroblasts compared to c ontrols (Fig. 4d, p=0.045). In contrast, in the p.R120W fibroblasts, no evidence of oxidative stress was observed (Fig. 4).
evidence.explanation: MitoSOX, thiol and antioxidant readouts support oxidative stress in C240Y-family fibroblasts, whereas R120W-family cells did not show the same response.

steps/7.description: Dominant-variant expression can increase mitochondrial ROS, and patient C240Y fibroblasts show increased MitoSOX signal with supporting oxidative-stress readouts. evidence.snippet: Disease onset varied widely, ranging from childhood to late adulthood. Walking difficulties were the most common initial symptoms. Disease progression was slow and as a rule patients remained ambulatory. Four patients (CMT-129.03, CMT-129.07, CMT-1060.01, and CMT-1130.03) required an ankle foot orthosis; patient CMT-1058.01 became wheelchair-dependent at the age of 61 years. Weakness and atrophy was mainly restricted to distal muscles of the lower and upper limbs except for patients CMT-129.03, CMT-129.07, CMT-1058.01, and CMT-1130.03, who had mild signs of proximal weakness.

evidence.snippet: In 8 Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT) families we identified 4 pathogenic heterozygous GDAP1 mutations, 3 of which are novel. Three of the mutations displayed reduced disease penetrance. Disease onset in the affected individuals was variable, ranging from early childhood to adulthood. Disease progression was slow in most patients and overall severity milder than typically seen in autosomal recessive GDAP1 mutations.
evidence.explanation: Eight ascertained families establish dominant inheritance and variable expression; seven families were recruited separately from the 97-family screening cohort.

evidence.snippet: We traced segregation of the GDAP1 mutations in all available family members and all clinically affected individuals carried a mutant allele. This analysis further identified 4 unaffected carriers of the His123Arg mutation in the first generation of the Finnish family (CMT-129).
evidence.explanation: Clinically unaffected carriers were identified by family genotyping.

evidence.snippet: We describe two unrelated Spanish families with a dominant axonal CMT. A novel in frame GAA deletion in exon 5 of the GDAP1 gene (c.677_679del; p.R226del) was identified in both families.
evidence.explanation: Two families carry an in-frame deletion; the precise source wording is checked against the abstract.

evidence.snippet: Three novel mutations were identified in three families with dominant segregation of the disease: two missense changes, p.Arg226Ser and p.Ser34Cys, affecting the GST domain of the GDAP1 protein and a novel deletion (c.23delAG) leading to early truncation of the protein upstream the GST domain.
evidence.explanation: This historical report includes an early truncating allele in a dominant family; it does not establish a general haploinsufficiency mechanism.

evidence.snippet: | 3 | GDAP1 c.811G > A (p.Gly271Arg), classified as pathogenic | Late 60s | Paresthesias and numbness in thumbs and toes, absent achilles reflexes | Normal | Father with neuropathy |
evidence.explanation: The table explicitly records the authors’ pathogenic classification of p.Gly271Arg; the separate p.Ala336Ser case is a VUS.

evidence.snippet: Families were described with Ser34Cys, Arg120Trp, Gln218Glu, Arg226Ser, and Cys240Tyr mutations, while Thr157Pro occurred de novo in a single patient.
evidence.explanation: This sentence summarizes previously reported alleles rather than additional families newly ascertained in the 2011 study.

genes/0.notes: Dominant disease has been reported with alleles including p.Arg120Trp, p.His123Arg, p.Ala156Gly, p.Pro274Leu, p.Gln218Glu, p.Arg226Lys and p.Gly271Arg. The 2022 sensory-predominant series classified p.Gly271Arg as pathogenic, whereas its p.Ala336Ser observation remained a VUS and does not establish a causal dominant allele. Earlier reports summarized by the 2011 cohort also include a de novo p.Thr157Pro observation. An in-frame p.Arg226del and a historically reported early truncating c.23delAG allele mean that the disorder should not be defined as missense-only. This catalogue is not a claim that all rare heterozygous GDAP1 variants are pathogenic. Reduced penetrance belongs to the causal GDAP1 record, not a second modifier-gene record. Variant position or soluble-fragment melting temperature is not a validated clinical severity predictor.

genes/1.notes: The p.Arg213Pro allele is a proposed modifier of GDAP1 p.Arg120Trp based on one double-carrier proband within a screen of 24 GDAP1 carriers from eight Spanish families. Cell experiments support context-dependent effects on store-operated calcium entry, but do not establish a broadly replicated human modifier association, JPH1-alone disease causation or a clinical calcium-directed treatment.

evidence.explanation: General CMT symptom guidance; no CMT2K-specific comparative response estimate.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Symptom-directed care is extrapolated from general CMT guidance; subtype-specific controlled efficacy has not been established.

evidence.snippet: Musculoskeletal pain may respond to acetaminophen or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents
evidence.explanation: General CMT symptomatic care recommendation.

treatments/5.description: Evaluate mechanical and musculoskeletal causes of pain and use appropriate analgesic and rehabilitative care. Current general CMT guidance lists acetaminophen and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents as options; no GDAP1-specific response is established.

evidence.snippet: Obesity is to be avoided because it makes walking more difficult.
evidence.explanation: General CMT mobility advice.

evidence.snippet: Chemotherapy for cancer that includes vincristine may be especially damaging to peripheral nerves and severely worsen CMT
evidence.explanation: General CMT medication precaution.

treatments/6.description: Support an appropriate weight to reduce mobility burden and review potentially neurotoxic medicines in the context of their clinical benefits and alternatives. Vincristine can markedly worsen peripheral neuropathy in CMT; this is a general CMT precaution, not evidence that such exposure causes inherited GDAP1 disease.

A reported severe case received bilevel positive airway pressure but subsequently deteriorated; this exposure does not establish a CMT2K-specific survival benefit. Hoarseness requires assessment rather than automatic attribution to vocal-fold paresis.
