evidence.snippet: Measles virus (MeV) may persist in the brain, causing fatal neurodegenerative diseases, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, and measles inclusion-body encephalitis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes CNS persistence of measles virus as the basis of the rare, fatal late complication SSPE.

steps/6.description: A rare, uniformly fatal late complication in which measles virus persists in the central nervous system and, after a latency of years, causes a progressive neurodegenerative panencephalitis.

edges/0.description: Infected macrophages and dendritic cells transport virus to lymphoid tissue where lymphocytes are infected.

edges/1.description: Infected immune cells deliver virus to the basolateral surface of airway epithelium.

edges/2.description: Viremic spread seeds the skin.

evidence.snippet: Measles is best prevented through vaccination, and the major reductions in measles incidence and mortality have renewed interest in regional elimination and global eradication.
evidence.explanation: Lancet seminar establishing vaccination as the primary prevention and driver of measles mortality reduction.

treatments/0.description: Live attenuated measles vaccine, given as the combined MMR vaccine, is the primary preventive measure and the basis for measles elimination programs.

evidence.snippet: two doses were associated with a reduced risk of mortality and pneumonia-specific mortality in children under the age of two years
evidence.explanation: Cochrane meta-analysis of randomized trials showing two-dose vitamin A reduces measles mortality in young children.

evidence.snippet: Children with low levels were more likely to have fever at a temperature of 40 degrees C or higher (68% vs 44%), to have fever for 7 days or more (54% vs 23%), and to be hospitalized (55% vs 30%).
evidence.explanation: Cohort study linking low vitamin A levels to more severe measles, supporting vitamin A repletion.

treatments/1.description: WHO recommends vitamin A for children with acute measles. Two-dose vitamin A reduces mortality and pneumonia-specific mortality in children under two, and low vitamin A levels are associated with more severe disease.

evidence.snippet: The management of patients with measles includes provision of vitamin A.
evidence.explanation: Lancet seminar summarizing supportive management of measles including vitamin A.

treatments/2.description: Symptomatic management with antipyretics, hydration, and treatment of secondary bacterial complications such as pneumonia and otitis media.

evidence.snippet: Most variants clustered closely around the zinc-binding residues of two zinc-finger domains (ZZ and TAZ2) and within the first α helix of the fourth intrinsically disordered linker (ID4) of CBP/p300.
evidence.explanation: Localizes the causal variants in 82 individuals to the zinc-binding residues and the ID4 helix.

evidence.snippet: Variants that produce a null allele or disrupt the catalytic domain of either protein cause Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome (RSTS), while pathogenic missense and in-frame indel variants in parts of exons 30 and 31 cause phenotypes recently described as Menke-Hennekam syndrome (MKHK).
evidence.explanation: Distinguishes the MKHK variant class from the null and catalytic-domain alleles of RSTS.

evidence.snippet: This study revealed that one frameshift and three nonsense variants of CREBBP cause MKHK1, and inferred that the nonsense variants of the last exon could further help in the elucidation of the etiology of MKHK1.
evidence.explanation: Reports truncating last-exon CREBBP variants with an MKHK1 phenotype, which qualifies the missense/in-frame description of the variant class.

steps/2.description: A heterozygous missense or in-frame indel variant alters one residue or a few residues in the C-terminal MKHK region of CBP or p300 (ZZ domain, TAZ2 domain, or the first helix of ID4). Unlike RSTS alleles, these variants are predicted to produce a full-length protein. Most cluster around the zinc-coordinating residues of the two zinc fingers or around ID4 residues predicted to hydrogen-bond with the HAT domain.

evidence.snippet: interaction of the ZZ domain with H3 promotes selective acetylation of the histone H3K27 and H3K18 sites
evidence.explanation: Establishes the normal function of the ZZ domain whose zinc-binding residues are the MKHK-ZZ variant hotspot; does not test patient variants.

evidence.snippet: The highest affinity interactions are between the intrinsically disordered N-terminal transactivation domain (TAD) of p53 and the TAZ1 and TAZ2 domains of CBP/p300.
evidence.explanation: TAZ2 is a high-affinity transcription-factor binding module; background for the interaction hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: we determine the disordered C-terminal region of β-catenin binds promiscuously to the TAZ1 and TAZ2 domains of CBP/p300
evidence.explanation: A further transcriptional regulator docking on TAZ2, illustrating the breadth of TAZ2 partners.

evidence.snippet: Structural modeling predicted that the NP_004371.2:p.(Cys1790Arg) substitution may disrupt the tertiary structure of the CBP TAZ2 domain (amino acids 1772-1840) when interacting with STAT1 but not with adenovirus E1A, potentially affecting transcription factor binding and disease phenotype.
evidence.explanation: In silico modeling of a patient TAZ2 variant predicting partner-selective disruption of the TAZ2 fold.

steps/3.description: The ZZ and TAZ2 zinc fingers are protein-interaction modules: the p300 ZZ domain reads the histone H3 tail and steers HAT activity toward H3K27 and H3K18, and TAZ2 binds the transactivation domains of many transcription factors (p53, beta-catenin, STAT1, adenovirus E1A) and also restrains the adjacent HAT domain. The first ID4 helix is predicted to contact the HAT domain. MKHK variants are proposed to perturb these folds and interfaces.

evidence.snippet: we hypothesize that the mutations disturb protein-protein interactions by altering zinc finger function
evidence.explanation: States the interaction hypothesis; no functional data.

steps/4.description: Proposed consequence of a misfolded TAZ2 or ZZ domain: CBP/p300 binds some of its transcription-factor partners abnormally, changing which genes are co-activated. Partner selectivity (for example STAT1 but not E1A for one TAZ2 variant) has only been predicted in silico.

evidence.snippet: Here, we demonstrate that p300/CBP is not only a transcriptional adaptor but also a histone acetyltransferase.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the intrinsic HAT activity of the affected proteins.

evidence.snippet: Here we show that CBP has intrinsic HAT activity.
evidence.explanation: Independent demonstration of CBP HAT activity.

evidence.snippet: We use NMR to investigate the structure of the complex and found that the TAZ2 domain has an autoinhibitory role for p300.
evidence.explanation: TAZ2, the MKHK-TAZ2 hotspot, restrains p300 HAT activity.

evidence.snippet: concluded that deletion of this region is not associated with a loss of enzymatic activity but rather with modulation of CBP substrate specificity, leading to non-specific acetylation of various proteins by CBP and a potential gain of function
evidence.explanation: The MKHK cohort paper's summary of a biochemical study (Sheahan et al.) of an engineered deletion of the ZZ/TAZ2/ID4 region; it did not test patient variants, and the underlying study is cited here through this summary.

steps/5.description: CBP and p300 are histone and protein acetyltransferases. The TAZ2 domain and the ID4 helix sit against the HAT domain and are proposed to regulate it, so MKHK variants could release autoinhibition or change substrate specificity rather than abolish catalysis. This is the gain-of-function hypothesis; it is supported by structural work on p300 and on engineered deletions of the region, and by the observation that MKHK faces resemble 16p13.3 duplication (CREBBP gain of dosage) rather than RSTS. No patient variant has been shown to increase HAT activity.

evidence.snippet: For the ID4 region in CBP/p300, a highly sensitive and specific episignature was refined (21 out of 21 individuals).
evidence.explanation: ID4 variants produce a robust blood episignature.

evidence.snippet: DNAm analysis identified two specific blood DNA methylation patterns (episignatures): RSTS and MKHK_IDR compared to matched normal controls. Samples with MKHK variants outside the IDR did not obey the MKHK_IDR episignature.
evidence.explanation: An independent cohort replicates a region-specific MKHK episignature distinct from RSTS, confined to the disordered-region variants.

steps/6.description: Genome-wide blood DNA methylation profiles that differ by affected region: a robust diagnostic episignature for ID4 variants (mean hypermethylation, opposite to RSTS) and milder, not yet diagnostic, profiles for ZZ and TAZ2 variants (preliminary mean hypomethylation). The episignatures are a readout of the molecular lesion used for diagnosis and variant classification, not a demonstrated cause of the clinical features.

evidence.snippet: By interrogating DNAm in hiPSCs of patients with RSTS and MKHK, we observed differentially methylated genes play a role in embryonic development and organogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Patient iPSC methylation changes fall on developmental genes; transcriptional consequences are inferred, not measured.

steps/7.description: Proposed convergent step: abnormal CBP/p300 co-activator function alters transcription of genes needed for embryonic development and organogenesis. Direct transcriptomic evidence in patient cells is lacking; the strongest current support is differential methylation of developmental genes in patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells.

evidence.snippet: Major malformations are less common except for cryptorchidism (46% of males), and cerebral anomalies (70%).
evidence.explanation: Structural cerebral anomalies are common, indicating abnormal brain development.

evidence.snippet: Our reports expand the clinical spectrum to include ventriculomegaly, absent corpus callosum, staphyloma, cochlear malformations, and exomphalos.
evidence.explanation: Adds brain malformations (ventriculomegaly, callosal agenesis) to the spectrum.

steps/8.description: Abnormal development of the brain, documented as structural cerebral anomalies (reported in about 70% of one cohort), including ventriculomegaly and callosal agenesis. No source links these anomalies, or a specific mechanism, to the developmental delay, intellectual disability, behavioral problems or epilepsy, so those phenotypes are not wired to this node. The cellular basis in neurons or neural progenitors has not been studied.

evidence.snippet: Major malformations are less common except for cryptorchidism (46% of males), and cerebral anomalies (70%).
evidence.explanation: Cerebral anomalies in 70% of the 2018 cohort, reported without further specification in the abstract.

steps/9.description: Structural cerebral anomalies of varied type; the cohort reports do not specify one predominant malformation.

evidence.snippet: Our reports expand the clinical spectrum to include ventriculomegaly, absent corpus callosum, staphyloma, cochlear malformations, and exomphalos.
evidence.explanation: Ventriculomegaly reported in an MKHK1 case series.

evidence.snippet: Our reports expand the clinical spectrum to include ventriculomegaly, absent corpus callosum, staphyloma, cochlear malformations, and exomphalos.
evidence.explanation: Callosal agenesis reported in an MKHK1 case series.

evidence.snippet: Variants in these domains were thus hypothesized to affect the coordinating properties of the two zinc-finger domains of CBP/p300 by affecting their proper folding.
evidence.explanation: States the folding hypothesis for zinc-finger variants; it is a hypothesis from variant position, not a functional result.

edges/6.description: Substitutions at or next to zinc-coordinating residues are expected to destabilize the zinc-finger fold; ID4 substitutions are predicted to disturb hydrogen bonds with the HAT domain. This is a structural prediction, not a measured effect.

evidence.snippet: No functional studies have (yet) been performed, but we hypothesize that the mutations disturb protein-protein interactions by altering zinc finger function.
evidence.explanation: The founding hypothesis that MKHK variants act by disturbing zinc-finger-mediated protein-protein interactions; explicitly untested.

evidence.snippet: NUT-TAZ2 interaction or mutations found in cancer that interfere with autoinhibition by TAZ2 allosterically activate p300.
evidence.explanation: Shows that disturbing TAZ2 autoinhibition activates p300 HAT activity. The mutations tested are cancer mutations, not MKHK variants, so the extrapolation to MKHK is indirect.

evidence.snippet: showed that the MKHK-ID4 episignature exhibits mean global DNA hypermethylation, contrary to the RSTS1 and RSTS2 episignatures
evidence.explanation: The methylation direction in MKHK-ID4 is opposite to RSTS, consistent with an effect opposite to loss of function; the link from HAT activity to the methylation pattern is inferred.

edges/13.description: The structural cerebral anomalies are the observable form of abnormal brain development in the cited cohort and case series.

evidence.snippet: By using exome sequencing, and by using Sanger in one patient, CREBBP mutations were detected in 11 patients who did not, or only in a very limited manner, resemble Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Gene discovery for the CREBBP form.

evidence.snippet: We report three further patients with de novo exon 31 CREBBP missense variants.
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation of de novo exon 31 CREBBP missense variants.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that there is now more firm evidence that variants in these specific regions of CREBBP and EP300 result in a phenotype that differs from RSTS, and that this phenotype may be heterogeneous.
evidence.explanation: Establishes EP300 variants in the homologous region as a cause.

evidence.snippet: a de novo germline missense variant (NM_001429.4: c.5258G>A, p.Cys1753Tyr) in the TAZ2 domain of EP300 from her buccal swab, which is consistent with a diagnosis of MKHK2
evidence.explanation: A de novo EP300 TAZ2 variant in an individual with MKHK2.

evidence.snippet: There is no specific treatment for this condition. The management of MHS cases requires a multidisciplinary team consisting of a maternal-fetal medicine specialist, pediatrician, geneticist, pediatric surgeon, pediatric neurologist, ophthalmologist, ENT specialist, nutritionist, and psychologist.
evidence.explanation: States that care is supportive and multidisciplinary.

treatments/0.description: There is no disease-specific treatment. Management is symptomatic and coordinated across pediatrics, genetics, neurology, ophthalmology, ENT, nutrition and psychology.

evidence.snippet: At the age of seven months the infant required gastrostomy as a result of persistent feeding difficulties with a low intake and consequent failure to thrive
evidence.explanation: Single case report of gastrostomy for MKHK feeding difficulties.

treatments/1.description: Tube feeding and gastrostomy for infants with persistent feeding difficulties and failure to thrive.

evidence.snippet: The patient was discharged with a nasogastric tube and followed a continuous physical therapy program.
evidence.explanation: Physical therapy used in an infant with MKHK (case report).

evidence.snippet: Following this diagnosis, early targeted interventions were initiated, including hearing aid fitting, enrollment in a comprehensive rehabilitation program, and planning for necessary surgical corrections.
evidence.explanation: Single case of hearing aid and rehabilitation after neonatal diagnosis.

treatments/3.description: Hearing aid fitting and enrollment in a comprehensive rehabilitation program after early molecular diagnosis; developmental improvement was reported at 15 months in one case, without a comparator.

evidence.snippet: The variants were reported de novo, with paternity having been confirmed, suggesting the occurrence of germline mosaicism in MKHK-ID4.
evidence.explanation: Germline mosaicism is the basis for recurrence-risk counseling after a de novo case; the source does not itself discuss counseling.

treatments/4.description: Counseling addresses autosomal dominant transmission, the predominantly de novo occurrence, and a residual recurrence risk from parental germline mosaicism, which has been observed in one MKHK-ID4 sibship.

evidence.snippet: No functional studies have (yet) been performed, but we hypothesize that the mutations disturb protein-protein interactions by altering zinc finger function.
evidence.explanation: Original statement of the interaction hypothesis.

hypotheses/0.description: MKHK variants misfold the ZZ or TAZ2 zinc fingers and change which transcription factors or histone tails CBP/p300 engage, altering co-activator output without removing the protein. Proposed from variant position and structural modeling; not tested with patient variants.

evidence.snippet: 3D face shape demonstrated resemblance to individuals with a duplication of 16p13.3 (the region that includes CREBBP), possibly indicating a gain of function.
evidence.explanation: Phenotypic argument for a gain-of-function mechanism.

evidence.snippet: These focus on functional impact of the presently reported variants in ZZ, TAZ2, and ID4 that are needed to confirm our hypothesis that variants in ID4 result in a gain of function.
evidence.explanation: The cohort authors state the gain-of-function hypothesis and that it is not yet confirmed.

hypotheses/1.description: MKHK variants, particularly in ID4 and TAZ2, relieve the restraint these regions place on the HAT domain or alter its substrate specificity, giving a gain of function that opposes the loss of function in RSTS. Supported indirectly by facial resemblance to 16p13.3 duplication, by opposite methylation direction to RSTS, and by structural studies of p300 autoinhibition; the cohort authors state that functional studies are needed to confirm it.

evidence.snippet: These focus on functional impact of the presently reported variants in ZZ, TAZ2, and ID4 that are needed to confirm our hypothesis that variants in ID4 result in a gain of function.
evidence.explanation: The cohort authors state the functional studies are still needed.

open_questions/0.rationale: No functional study of patient variants has been published. The two hypotheses rest on variant position, structural modeling, facial similarity to 16p13.3 duplication, methylation direction, and biochemistry of cancer mutations or engineered deletions. The subtype-specific phenotypes and methylation profiles suggest the mechanism may differ by domain, and truncating last-exon variants with an MKHK-like phenotype further complicate a single explanation.

evidence.snippet: Phenotypes including intellectual disability of varying degree and distinct physical features were defined for each of the regions.
evidence.explanation: Phenotypes differ by variant region, but the paper defines them clinically without a mechanism for any single feature.

open_questions/1.rationale: The published literature on MKHK is clinical delineation (case reports and cohorts) plus blood and iPSC methylation profiling. No study connects a molecular or cellular change to any specific clinical feature, and no animal or cellular model of an MKHK variant has been reported in the sources cited here. Apart from the structural brain anomalies, the phenotypes are therefore left without an upstream mechanism node. The subtype-specific features (overweight and hypermetropia in MKHK-ZZ; muscle hypertrophy, contractures and clubfeet in MKHK-TAZ2 and MKHK-ID4) suggest domain-specific downstream pathways.

evidence.snippet: Using microcell-mediated chromosome transfer and exome sequencing, we identified causal mutations in ABCD4, a gene that codes for an ABC transporter, which was previously thought to have peroxisomal localization and function.
evidence.explanation: The gene-disease assignment from the study that made it, and the statement that the protein's localisation was reassigned as a result.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, we show that mutations altering the putative ATPase domain of ABCD4 affect its function, suggesting that the ATPase activity of ABCD4 may be involved in intracellular processing of vitamin B12.
evidence.explanation: Locates the functional defect at the ATPase domain. Note the authors' own hedging - "suggesting" and "may be involved" - which is preserved rather than firmed up in the node description.

steps/1.description: Biallelic loss-of-function variation in ABCD4, an ATP-binding cassette transporter. Notably, ABCD4 was assumed to be a peroxisomal protein until this disease was described - the subfamily assignment predicted peroxisomal localisation, and the disease is what showed it acts at the lysosome. Several reported variants alter the ATPase domain, which is the part of the transporter that would supply the energy for the export step.

evidence.snippet: While most lysosomal membrane proteins are directed to the lysosome via sorting motifs, the cobalamin exporter ABCD4 is distinct, instead relying on LMBD1 as a dedicated chaperone for its trafficking.
evidence.explanation: States why the two proteins are interdependent rather than merely associated: ABCD4 lacks the usual sorting motif and reaches the lysosome only as LMBD1 cargo. This is the structural basis for the phenocopy relationship between cblJ and cblF that the entry treats as a curation boundary question.

evidence.snippet: Cell imaging shows that disruption of these interactions impairs the trafficking of ABCD4 to lysosomes.
evidence.explanation: The functional test of the structural claim, and the direct support for this node's assertion that a complex which does not assemble does not reach the lysosome.

evidence.snippet: Using a sensitive live-cell FRET assay, we demonstrated selective interaction between ABCD4 and LMBD1 and decreased interaction when ABCD4 harbored the patient mutations p.Arg432Gln or p.Asn141Lys or when artificial mutations disrupted the ATPase domain.
evidence.explanation: The direct measurement that patient variants reduce the protein-protein interaction. This is the mechanistic core of the node, and it is measured in a heterologous live-cell system rather than in patient tissue.

evidence.snippet: Finally, we showed that ABCD4 lysosomal targeting depends on co-expression of, and interaction with, LMBD1.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the directional dependence - ABCD4 needs LMBD1 to reach the lysosome at all, which is a stronger claim than mere partnership.

evidence.snippet: Our results show that ABCD4 colocalizes with the lysosomal proteins LAMP1 and LMBD1, the latter of which is deficient in the cblF defect.
evidence.explanation: The colocalisation evidence placing ABCD4 on the lysosome next to the cblF protein, which is what put the two diseases in the same mechanism.

steps/2.description: ABCD4 does not work alone. It interacts selectively with LMBD1, and its delivery to the lysosome depends on that interaction - without LMBD1 co-expression, ABCD4 is not targeted correctly. Patient missense variants reduce the interaction directly, measured by live-cell FRET. This interdependence is the mechanistic explanation for something clinicians had already noticed: cblJ and cblF are indistinguishable at the bedside because they are two ways of breaking one complex.

evidence.snippet: We describe a new disease that results in failure to release vitamin B12 from lysosomes, which mimics the cblF defect caused by LMBRD1 mutations.
evidence.explanation: States the defining cellular lesion and, in the same sentence, the phenocopy relationship with cblF that this entry treats as a curation boundary question.

evidence.snippet: The integral membrane proteins LMBD1 and ABCD4 are required for lysosomal release of Cbl, and mutations in the genes LMBRD1 and ABCD4 result in the cobalamin metabolism disorders cblF and cblJ.
evidence.explanation: States the transport step and assigns each gene to its complementation group.

steps/3.description: Cobalamin taken up by the cell is trapped in the lysosome. Everything downstream is starved of substrate even though total cellular cobalamin may be normal or high, which is why the biochemistry of this disease looks like severe B12 deficiency in a patient whose serum B12 can be unremarkable. Free cobalamin accumulates in the lysosome rather than reaching the cytosolic processing enzymes.

evidence.snippet: Cbl cofactor forms are decreased in fibroblasts from this patient but could be rescued by overexpression of either ABCD4 or, unexpectedly, LMBD1.
evidence.explanation: The direct measurement of cofactor depletion in patient cells, together with the rescue that confirms it is caused by the transport defect. The cross-rescue by LMBD1 is the surprising part, and it supports the complex model asserted on the node above.

evidence.snippet: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin (Cbl)), in the cofactor forms methyl-Cbl and adenosyl-Cbl, is required for the function of the essential enzymes methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, respectively.
evidence.explanation: States the cofactor-to-enzyme assignments on which both downstream edges of this node depend. Graded OTHER, not HUMAN_CLINICAL - this is background biochemistry from the paper's introduction, established long before this study and not an observation the study made.

steps/4.description: Adenosylcobalamin and methylcobalamin are both reduced, because both are made from cytosolic cobalamin downstream of the failed export step. This simultaneous depletion is the branch point that produces the combined biochemical phenotype, and it is the reason a single transport defect looks like two different enzyme deficiencies at once.

steps/5.description: Without adenosylcobalamin, mitochondrial methylmalonyl-CoA mutase cannot convert methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. Methylmalonic acid accumulates and is excreted.

steps/6.description: Without methylcobalamin, cytosolic methionine synthase cannot remethylate homocysteine to methionine. Homocysteine accumulates and methionine synthesis falls, so this arm is a remethylation defect rather than a transsulfuration one.

evidence.snippet: Described clinical features include feeding difficulties, failure to thrive, hypotonia, seizures, developmental delay, and hematological abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: The summary of the reported clinical picture, drawn from the symptomatic probands that make up nearly all published cases.

steps/7.description: The clinical layer. Feeding difficulty, failure to thrive, hypotonia, seizures and developmental delay together with haematological abnormality, presenting in the neonatal period or infancy. The entry does not attempt to route each of these to one or other biochemical arm, because no published study separates them - both arms are impaired simultaneously in every patient.

evidence.snippet: who presented at 7 days of age with poor feeding, hypotonia, methylmalonic aciduria, and elevated plasma homocysteine
evidence.explanation: Documents the finding in a reported patient, alongside the age at presentation.

steps/8.description: Elevated methylmalonic acid in urine and plasma, from the blocked adenosylcobalamin arm.

evidence.snippet: an ultra-rare autosomal recessive disorder of intracellular cobalamin metabolism associated with combined methylmalonic acidemia and homocystinuria
evidence.explanation: States that the combined pattern is the defining biochemical characteristic of the disease.

steps/9.description: Homocysteine accumulation from the blocked methylcobalamin arm, raised in both plasma and urine. Its presence alongside methylmalonic aciduria is what distinguishes the combined disorders from isolated methylmalonic acidemia. The bound term is the urinary finding; plasma total homocysteine is the measurement clinical practice actually uses, and it is curated as a biomarker in the biochemical section rather than duplicated here as a second phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Described clinical features include feeding difficulties, failure to thrive, hypotonia, seizures, developmental delay, and hematological abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Lists hypotonia among the reported features.

steps/10.description: Reduced muscle tone, present from the neonatal period in symptomatic patients.

evidence.snippet: feeding difficulties, failure to thrive, hypotonia, seizures, developmental delay, and hematological abnormalities
evidence.explanation: Lists seizures among the reported features. The source gives no proportion, which is why the frequency is VARIABLE.

steps/11.description: Reported among the neurological features of symptomatic patients.

evidence.snippet: Described clinical features include feeding difficulties, failure to thrive, hypotonia, seizures, developmental delay, and hematological abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Lists developmental delay among the reported features of symptomatic patients.

evidence.snippet: With early detection and initiation of treatment, this patient has remained asymptomatic with normal growth parameters and neurodevelopmental function.
evidence.explanation: Graded REFUTE against developmental delay being an inevitable feature of the disease. The same paper supplies both items, which is the point - it reports the historical picture and then a counterexample to it.

steps/12.description: Reported in symptomatic patients, and explicitly absent in the one patient detected and treated presymptomatically.

evidence.snippet: Described clinical features include feeding difficulties, failure to thrive, hypotonia, seizures, developmental delay, and hematological abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Names failure to thrive directly, in the summary of the reported cblJ series. This is the tighter match for the phenotype as named; the poor-feeding observation below is the individual-case correlate.

evidence.snippet: who presented at 7 days of age with poor feeding, hypotonia
evidence.explanation: Documents poor feeding as a presenting feature at one week of age, in a single patient.

steps/13.description: Poor feeding and failure to thrive, typically the presenting problem in the neonatal period.

evidence.snippet: At the age of 8 years, the patient developed megaloblastic anemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency, leading to the initiation of replacement therapy.
evidence.explanation: The one cblJ-specific documentation of the phenotype, with its age of onset and its diagnostic consequence.

evidence.snippet: cytopenias (including megaloblastic anemia), global developmental delay, encephalopathy, and neurologic signs such as hypotonia and seizures
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews group-level statement. It describes the intracellular cobalamin disorders as a class, with cblC as the prototype, so it supports the phenotype belonging to this disease group rather than establishing a cblJ-specific frequency.

steps/14.description:
Megaloblastic anemia from impaired methionine synthase and the resulting folate trap. Documented specifically in one cblJ patient, in whom it appeared at eight years of age and was the finding that finally led to cobalamin replacement after seven years of undiagnosed pain attacks.
Graded VARIABLE rather than FREQUENT, corrected in review. The only cblJ-specific documentation is that single patient; everything else is a group-level statement about the intracellular cobalamin disorders with cblC as prototype. That is the same evidence shape carried by Seizures and Developmental delay, both VARIABLE here, and weaker than the shape behind Hypotonia and Failure to thrive, which are named in a cblJ case-series sentence. A FREQUENT grade would have imported a class-level frequency into a disease with eight reported patients.

evidence.snippet: The patient, a 15-year-old male of Azerbaijani descent, presented with severe abdominal pain beginning at the age of 1 year. These episodic pain attacks were accompanied by hypotonia, pallor, nausea, and vomiting.
evidence.explanation: The presentation, with its age of onset and accompanying features. One patient, which is why the frequency is VARIABLE.

evidence.snippet: The pain attacks ceased during treatment but recurred whenever vitamin B12 levels dropped after discontinuation.
evidence.explanation: A within-patient withdrawal and rechallenge. It is the strongest causal evidence in this entry that a clinical feature is driven by the cobalamin deficit rather than merely co-occurring with it, and it is n=1.

steps/15.description: Episodic severe abdominal pain with hypotonia, pallor, nausea and vomiting, reported from the age of one year in a single patient who had none of the neurological features that define the usual presentation. It is curated because the diagnostic lesson is unusually sharp: seven years of inconclusive evaluation followed, and the disease was found only when anemia appeared.

evidence.snippet: we report on a 12-year-old girl from Taiwan with a 6-year history of diffuse progressive skin hyperpigmentation resulting from a different aetiology
evidence.explanation: A single case, which is why the frequency is VARIABLE. The presentation is atypical in both feature and age, and the patient had no neurological signs.

steps/16.description: Diffuse progressive hyperpigmentation, reported as the dominant presenting feature in one patient with an otherwise mild course. It is recorded because it is the feature most likely to lead down a wrong diagnostic pathway, having been worked up as a pigmentary disorder.

edges/2.description: The variants act by preventing the transporter from assembling with, or being targeted alongside, its partner protein.

edges/3.description: The complex is the exporter, so a complex that does not assemble or does not reach the lysosome cannot export.

edges/4.description: The cytosolic processing that generates both cofactors cannot start on cobalamin that never leaves the lysosome.

edges/5.description: Adenosylcobalamin is the cofactor of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, so its depletion blocks that reaction.

edges/6.description: Methylcobalamin is the cofactor of methionine synthase, so its depletion blocks that reaction.

edges/7.description: Both cofactor arms fail together, and the clinical picture follows from the pair rather than from either one. The edge is drawn from this node rather than from the two enzyme-failure nodes below it for that reason: no published study in this disease separates the neurological and haematological consequences by arm, and drawing two edges would assert an attribution nobody has made.

edges/8.description: The accumulated acid is excreted, and is what the newborn screen and the urine organic acid profile detect.

edges/9.description: Accumulated homocysteine is excreted and raises plasma total homocysteine.

edges/10.description: Part of the reported neurological picture. Indirect because the intermediate steps between cofactor depletion and the neurological deficit are not established in this disease.

edges/11.description: Part of the reported neurological picture, with the same caveat about intermediates.

edges/12.description: Reported in the symptomatic probands. Note the entry also carries REFUTE evidence that this is not inevitable, from the presymptomatically treated patient.

edges/13.description: Poor feeding and failure to thrive, typically the presenting problem.

edges/14.description: The haematological half of this node, through impaired methionine synthase and the consequent folate trap. The trap itself is not separately modelled because no cited source in this entry measures it here.

edges/15.description: Reported as the dominant and near-isolated presentation in one patient. The edge is drawn because the attacks ceased on cobalamin and recurred when levels fell, which is a within-patient rechallenge tying them to the cofactor deficit rather than to a coincidental cause.

edges/16.description: Reported as the dominant presenting feature in one patient with an otherwise mild course. The mechanism linking cobalamin deficiency to hyperpigmentation is not established.

evidence.snippet: By this approach, a homozygous mutation, c.423C>G, in the ABCD4 gene was identified.
evidence.explanation: A causal variant identified in an individual patient, from the report that also established that the presentation can be late-onset.

evidence.snippet: A novel homozygous missense variant, c.1591C>T (p.Arg531Trp) in exon 17 of ABCD4, was identified.
evidence.explanation: The second causal allele curated here, from the 2025 report. Added in review - the variant was cited elsewhere in the entry while the record whose job is to list alleles did not carry it.

evidence.snippet: The arginine at codon 531 is located in the ABC transporter domain
evidence.explanation: Locates the residue in the transporter domain, which is what makes the variant mechanistically interpretable rather than only a reported allele.

genes/0.notes: An ATP-binding cassette transporter of the D subfamily. Its assignment to the lysosome rather than the peroxisome came out of this disease rather than preceding it, which is a good example of a rare disease correcting a protein annotation. Reported alleles include ATPase-domain missense variants (p.Arg432Gln, p.Asn141Lys), the ABC-transporter-domain missense variant p.Arg531Trp, and frameshifts.

evidence.snippet: With early detection and initiation of treatment, this patient has remained asymptomatic with normal growth parameters and neurodevelopmental function.
evidence.explanation: A single patient followed to 17 months. It is an outcome under early treatment with no comparator, so it supports treatment being compatible with a normal course rather than demonstrating that treatment caused it.

evidence.snippet: Treatment with oral cobalamin (3 mg daily) led to metabolic correction and some reduction in the skin hyperpigmentation at the 3-month follow-up.
evidence.explanation: Records a biochemical and clinical response in a single patient, and notably by the oral route rather than parenterally. The route matters mechanistically and this is the only report of it, so it is not generalised in the description above.

evidence.snippet: Betaine as first-line therapy for methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase deficiency and parenteral hydroxocobalamin for cobalamin-related defects have reduced mortality and morbidity.
evidence.explanation: The statement that actually supports the therapeutic_agent binding: neither cblJ-specific snippet above names hydroxocobalamin, and this one does. Graded INDIRECT because it is class-level guidance for cobalamin-related defects rather than a cblJ result, and OTHER because it is consensus guideline text rather than a study.

evidence.snippet: Early institution of injectable hydroxocobalamin improves survival and may reduce but not completely prevent primary manifestations.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews management statement, and the reason this entry treats early treatment as the intervention that matters. Note the hedge the chapter itself carries - reduce but not completely prevent - which is consistent with the one cblJ patient who stayed well and the several who did not.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Prolonged fasting (longer than overnight without dextrose-containing intravenous fluids); dietary protein intake below the recommended dietary allowance for age or more than that prescribed by a metabolic specialist; methionine restriction including use of medical foods that do not contain methionine; and the anesthetic nitrous oxide.
evidence.explanation: The agents and circumstances to avoid. Nitrous oxide is the one worth reading twice: it inactivates cobalamin directly, so a routine anaesthetic is a specific hazard in a patient whose cobalamin handling is already the lesion.

treatments/0.description:
Pharmacological cobalamin is the mainstay of treatment for the combined cobalamin disorders. The mechanistic rationale is that raising cobalamin availability drives enough of it past an impaired - rather than absent - lysosomal export step to supply the downstream cofactors.
The evidence in this specific disease is thin, and this record says so rather than importing the confidence that treating cblC would carry. What is published is that a presymptomatically treated patient stayed well, which is an outcome under treatment rather than a demonstration of effect, and that one late-presenting patient given oral cobalamin showed metabolic correction.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Raises the cobalamin concentration presented to a transport step that is impaired rather than absent, which is the rationale for pharmacological rather than physiological dosing.

open_questions/0.rationale:
The published clinical picture - seizures, developmental delay, failure to thrive - comes from patients who were found because they were unwell. Two reports break that pattern in opposite ways and both matter. One patient came to attention at twelve years old with progressive skin hyperpigmentation and no neurological signs at all. Another was found on the newborn screen, treated from birth, and remained asymptomatic and neurotypical at 17 months.
With eight patients in total, three atypical or presymptomatic cases are a large fraction of the evidence base, and they suggest the severity in the literature is at least partly an ascertainment effect. This is recorded rather than resolved. Seventeen months of follow-up is not enough to say that early treatment prevents the neurological phenotype, and one late-presenting patient does not establish a mild end of the spectrum. What can be said is that the frequencies attached to the neurological phenotypes in this entry describe symptomatic probands, not all people with biallelic ABCD4 variants.

open_questions/1.rationale:
cblJ was described as mimicking cblF, and the mechanism explains why. The two proteins form one complex, ABCD4 needs LMBD1 to reach the lysosome, and overexpressing either one rescues the cofactor deficit in ABCD4-mutant fibroblasts. Nothing published separates the two groups on phenotype, and the separation is made by complementation or sequencing.
That leaves a real question rather than a settled answer. If ABCD4 supplies the ATPase activity and LMBD1 the targeting, the two defects need not be functionally identical, and a difference might show up in the degree of residual export or in response to pharmacological cobalamin. Nobody has looked with enough patients to tell. Until someone does, the two diseases should be curated as separate entries with a shared mechanism rather than merged, because the genes are distinct and the complementation groups are established.

evidence.snippet: Screening of this gene on genomic DNA revealed a mutation that interferes with correct splicing and results in the skipping of exon 2.
evidence.explanation: The founding allele and its consequence for the transcript.

evidence.snippet: No protein or transcript was found, making it a null mutation.
evidence.explanation: What makes the founding allele a null rather than a hypomorph. Graded OTHER because this review is restating the 2008 paper's result rather than reporting its own.

evidence.snippet: Biochemical analysis confirmed a complex I deficiency, and whole-exome sequencing revealed a homozygous mutation in NDUFA2 (c.134A>C, p.Lys45Thr).
evidence.explanation: The recurrent missense allele, in the patient in whom it is homozygous, and the biochemistry that preceded its identification.

steps/1.description: Two damaged copies of NDUFA2. Four patients and four alleles are known and they fall into two classes. The founding case is homozygous for the splice variant c.208+5G>A, which causes most transcripts to skip exon 2 with a frameshift; no protein or transcript was detected, so it behaves as a null. The three later patients carry missense alleles at residues that contact NDUFS1 - p.Lys45Thr, homozygous in one and in trans with the frameshift p.Asn76Metfs*4 in another, and p.Glu57Ala homozygous in the fourth.

evidence.snippet: This subunit is bound to the matrix arm in a unique fashion, with exclusive contacts to core subunit NDUFS1.
evidence.explanation: The architectural fact the node rests on: a single binding partner, so a variant at that interface has one thing it can disrupt.

evidence.snippet: Lys45 is found at the interface with NDUFS1 and has close contacts with several NDUFS1 residues, including Gly376, Asp380, and Ser672.
evidence.explanation: The structural placement of the recurrent missense residue. Graded COMPUTATIONAL because it is an analysis of published structures rather than a measurement on patient material.

evidence.snippet: It is likely that the binding of NDUFA2 to NDUFS1 is destabilized.
evidence.explanation: The inference itself, with the hedge the source puts on it. This sentence is why the node is PROVISIONAL rather than ESTABLISHED.

evidence.snippet: This residue is at the interface with NDUFS1 and makes a possible ion pair with Arg382 of NDUFS1.
evidence.explanation: The second missense residue, mapped to the same interface, which is what makes the two independent patient alleles a converging argument rather than two isolated predictions.

steps/2.description: NDUFA2 binds the matrix arm through a single interface. It has exclusive contacts with the core subunit NDUFS1, made mostly through the flat four-stranded beta-sheet of its thioredoxin-like fold, and it sits at least 40 angstroms from any iron-sulfur cluster - so it cannot be doing chemistry, and what it can be doing is holding NDUFS1 in place. Both patient missense residues map to that interface: Lys45 contacts several NDUFS1 residues directly, and Glu57 makes a probable ion pair with NDUFS1 Arg382. The reading is that these alleles weaken the contact rather than remove the protein.

evidence.snippet: In culture, NDUFA2 knockout cell lines have been found to lack complex I activity, and an analysis by blue native (BN) gel electrophoresis showed a limited assembly of the N-module
evidence.explanation: The assembly defect and which module it hits. Graded OTHER because the review is restating a knockout study it cites, and INDIRECT because the system is an engineered cell line rather than patient material.

evidence.snippet: Complex I activity has been found to be extremely low, consistent with a missing NADH binding site
evidence.explanation: Connects the missing module to the lost function: the N-module is where NADH is oxidised, so its absence explains the size of the activity deficit.

evidence.snippet: The mutation in this accessory subunit causes reduced activity and disturbed assembly of complex I.
evidence.explanation: The same two consequences - activity and assembly - in the patient rather than the cell line, and the sentence that makes this an assembly disease rather than a catalytic one.

steps/3.description: Losing NDUFA2 does not just weaken complex I, it prevents part of it from being built. In knockout cell lines, blue native electrophoresis shows the N-module only partly assembled, with the core subunits NDUFS1, NDUFV1 and NDUFV2 lost along with the accessory subunits NDUFS4, NDUFS6, NDUFA7 and NDUFV3. The N-module carries the NADH binding site, which is why activity falls further than the amount of residual complex would suggest. In the founding patient the same effect was described as disturbed assembly of complex I.

evidence.snippet: We report a patient with an isolated complex I deficiency expressed in skin fibroblasts as well as muscle tissue.
evidence.explanation: The deficiency, its isolation to complex I, and the two tissues in which it was demonstrated.

evidence.snippet: We report 2 patients with cystic leukoencephalopathy and complex I deficiency with recessive mutations in NDUFA2, an accessory subunit of complex I.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the biochemical phenotype in the second and third patients, and names NDUFA2's role as an accessory rather than a core subunit.

steps/4.description: The measured biochemical endpoint, and the phenotype the entity is named for. The founding patient's deficiency was expressed in both skin fibroblasts and muscle, and it was isolated - the other respiratory chain complexes were spared, which is what a subunit dedicated to complex I predicts and what distinguishes this from the combined deficiencies caused by defects of mitochondrial gene expression. Transducing the patient's cells with a baculovirus expressing wild-type NDUFA2 partially restored complex I expression and activity, which is the experiment that makes the gene causal rather than merely associated.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, the mutation is associated with a mitochondrial depolarization.
evidence.explanation: The cellular consequence, measured in patient fibroblasts.

steps/5.description: The consequence measured in the founding patient's fibroblasts. Complex I is one of the proton pumps that build the inner membrane potential, so an enzyme that cannot oxidise NADH cannot pump, and the membrane depolarises. The depolarisation was corrected along with the enzyme when wild-type NDUFA2 was supplied, which ties it to the genotype rather than to the culture.

evidence.snippet: An individual with Leigh syndrome and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy was discovered to be homozygous with a mutation, c.208 + 5 G > A, in the NDUFA2 gene that caused a reduction in correct splicing
evidence.explanation: The two organs affected in the founding case, with the allele. Graded OTHER because this review restates the 2008 report rather than presenting its own patient.

evidence.snippet: This is the first report of cystic leukoencephalopathy caused by mutations in NDUFA2.
evidence.explanation: The other tissue pattern, and the point at which the entity stopped being a Leigh syndrome gene in the literature.

steps/6.description: The tissues that fail are the ones with the least metabolic reserve. In the founding patient this was brain and heart - Leigh disease with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, ending in cardiovascular arrest before the age of one. In the three later patients it was brain alone, presenting as white matter disease rather than as the symmetrical brainstem and basal ganglia lesions of Leigh syndrome. Which of the two patterns a patient gets is unexplained, and the correlation with allele class is discussed rather than asserted.

evidence.snippet: We report a patient with an isolated complex I deficiency expressed in skin fibroblasts as well as muscle tissue.
evidence.explanation: The finding in the founding patient, in two tissues.

evidence.snippet: We report 2 patients with cystic leukoencephalopathy and complex I deficiency with recessive mutations in NDUFA2, an accessory subunit of complex I.
evidence.explanation: The same finding in the two 2018 patients.

steps/7.description: The defining biochemical finding, demonstrated in fibroblasts and in muscle in the founding patient and in the two leukoencephalopathy patients. It is isolated, meaning the other respiratory chain complexes are normal.

evidence.snippet: We report 2 patients with cystic leukoencephalopathy and complex I deficiency with recessive mutations in NDUFA2, an accessory subunit of complex I.
evidence.explanation: Two of the three patients with white matter disease, and its cystic character.

evidence.snippet: Herein, we report a further female child affected by NDUFA2-related disorder presenting with cavitating and tigroid-like pattern of leukodystrophy and without systemic biochemical abnormalities of mitochondrial disorders.
evidence.explanation: The third patient with white matter disease, its radiological pattern, and the negative that is worth carrying with it - no systemic biochemical abnormality.

steps/8.description: White matter disease is the modal presentation of NDUFA2 deficiency, present in three of the four reported patients. It has been described as cystic in the two 2018 cases and as cavitating with a tigroid-like pattern in the 2020 case.

evidence.snippet: Only 1 other patient with mutations in NDUFA2 and a different phenotype (Leigh syndrome) has previously been reported.
evidence.explanation: The Leigh presentation and its isolation to one patient, stated by the authors of the paper that established the alternative phenotype.

evidence.snippet: An individual with Leigh syndrome and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy was discovered to be homozygous with a mutation, c.208 + 5 G > A, in the NDUFA2 gene that caused a reduction in correct splicing
evidence.explanation: The same case with its allele attached, which is what makes the allele-phenotype question in the discussions block askable.

steps/9.description: The presentation of the founding patient, and the reason the entity entered the literature as a Leigh syndrome gene. It has not recurred in any patient since.

evidence.snippet: but also exhibited developmental regression and cystic leukoencephalopathy, and an additional diagnosis of complex I deficiency was suspected
evidence.explanation: Regression and white matter disease in the same patient, and the sequence in which the diagnoses were made.

steps/10.description: Loss of acquired skills, reported in the first of the two 2018 patients alongside her cystic leukoencephalopathy.

evidence.snippet: She developed focal epilepsy at six years, was wheelchair-bound at nine years, and was last evaluated at 12 years.
evidence.explanation: The first of the two patients with seizures. Graded OTHER because the review is restating the 2018 report.

evidence.snippet: This individual had abnormal white matter in the brain, microcephaly, seizures, and movement disorders.
evidence.explanation: The second of the two patients with seizures, reported without a type.

steps/11.description: Seizures of any type, in two of the four reported patients - the first 2018 patient, whose epilepsy is characterised as focal, and the 2020 patient, whose seizures are reported without a type.

evidence.snippet: She developed focal epilepsy at six years, was wheelchair-bound at nine years, and was last evaluated at 12 years.
evidence.explanation: The seizure type, its age of onset and the loss of ambulation, in the only patient with a documented course. Graded OTHER because the review is restating the 2018 report.

steps/12.description: Focal epilepsy beginning at six years in the first 2018 patient, who was wheelchair-bound by nine and last evaluated at twelve.

evidence.snippet: She also had movement difficulties and was last evaluated at age four.
evidence.explanation: The second 2018 patient. Graded OTHER because the review is restating the 2018 report rather than reporting its own observation.

evidence.snippet: This individual had abnormal white matter in the brain, microcephaly, seizures, and movement disorders.
evidence.explanation: The 2020 patient, in whom a movement disorder is reported alongside seizures.

steps/13.description: Two of the four reported patients have a movement abnormality: the second 2018 patient, described as having movement difficulties at her last evaluation at four years, and the 2020 patient, described as having movement disorders at the same age.

evidence.snippet: She developed focal epilepsy at six years, was wheelchair-bound at nine years, and was last evaluated at 12 years.
evidence.explanation: Loss of independent ambulation by nine years in the only patient with a documented motor course. Graded OTHER because the review is restating the 2018 report.

steps/14.description: The first 2018 patient, who developed focal epilepsy at six years, was wheelchair-bound by nine and last evaluated at twelve. This is the only patient in the series with a documented ambulation outcome.

evidence.snippet: An individual with Leigh syndrome and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy was discovered to be homozygous with a mutation, c.208 + 5 G > A, in the NDUFA2 gene that caused a reduction in correct splicing
evidence.explanation: The cardiac phenotype and the allele in the same sentence. Graded OTHER because it is the review restating the 2008 case.

steps/15.description: Reported in the founding patient alongside Leigh disease, and the proximate cause of his death. It has not been reported in any of the three later patients.

evidence.snippet: This individual had abnormal white matter in the brain, microcephaly, seizures, and movement disorders.
evidence.explanation: The 2020 patient's features, listed together. Graded OTHER because the review is restating the 2020 case report, whose own abstract describes only the leukodystrophy pattern.

steps/16.description: Reported in the 2020 patient, alongside white matter disease, seizures and movement disorder.

edges/2.description: The route taken by the two interface missense alleles, which leave the protein in place and weaken its grip on NDUFS1.

evidence.snippet: No protein or transcript was found, making it a null mutation.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the founding allele removes the protein outright, which is what distinguishes this edge from the missense route through the contact node.

edges/3.description: The route taken by the founding splice allele, which is a demonstrated null - no protein and no transcript were detected, so there is no NDUFA2 left to destabilise a contact with. Absence of the subunit reaches the assembly failure directly rather than through the interface node, which is why the two edges run in parallel.

evidence.snippet: The mutation in this accessory subunit causes reduced activity and disturbed assembly of complex I.
evidence.explanation: The gene-disease relationship as first established, and the mechanism class it belongs to.

evidence.snippet: The gene for NDUFA2 is located on chromosome 5. The protein contains 99 amino acids with a mass of about 10.9 kDa before the processing of the amino-terminal methionine.
evidence.explanation: The gene's location and the protein's size, from a structural review of the subunit.

genes/0.notes:
NDUFA2 is on chromosome 5 and encodes a 99-residue, roughly 10.9 kDa accessory subunit of complex I, also known as B8. It is not catalytic: it has a compact thioredoxin-like fold with a flat four-stranded beta-sheet, sits on the matrix arm, and lies at least 40 angstroms from any iron-sulfur cluster. Two cysteines sit in the loops of the sheet but are not oxidised in the available mammalian complex I structures, so the thioredoxin resemblance is structural rather than functional.
A caution for anyone extending this entry from the gene rather than from the disease. A homozygous NDUFA2 p.Asp50Asn was reported in one individual in a breast cancer screen; the residue is not at the NDUFS1 interface and the significance is explicitly uncertain. It is not a mitochondrial disease allele and is not curated here.

evidence.snippet: No protein or transcript was found, making it a null mutation.
evidence.explanation: The severe end of the proposed relationship - a demonstrated null.

evidence.snippet: It is likely that the binding of NDUFA2 to NDUFS1 is destabilized.
evidence.explanation: The milder end, and its status: a structural inference with the hedge intact. Graded COMPUTATIONAL because it is drawn from a structure rather than measured.

open_questions/0.rationale:
Four patients, two phenotypes, and a suspiciously tidy correspondence with allele class.
The one patient with Leigh disease and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, who died at eleven months, is homozygous for a splice allele in which neither protein nor transcript was detectable - a demonstrated null. The three patients with leukodystrophy who survived into childhood carry missense alleles at the NDUFS1 interface, or one such allele in trans with a frameshift, and the structural reading of those is a weakened contact rather than an absent protein. Residual function explaining severity is the obvious hypothesis and it is consistent with everything published.
Three things stop it being an answer. Nobody has quantified residual NDUFA2 protein or residual complex I activity in the missense patients, so "hypomorphic" is a structural inference and not a measurement; the one patient with a compound heterozygous genotype carries a frameshift on the other allele, which should place her closer to the null end than her phenotype does; and four patients across three laboratories and twelve years are not a genotype-phenotype series. It is also worth noting that the review from which the structural argument comes describes the p.Lys45Thr patient's course in detail while the primary report's abstract does not, so the clinical and structural claims here rest partly on a secondary source.
What would settle it is unglamorous and cheap: complex I activity, assembled complex I and NDUFA2 abundance measured in one laboratory in fibroblasts from a null patient and a missense patient side by side.

evidence.snippet: The first patient was initially diagnosed with a primary systemic carnitine deficiency associated with a homozygous variant in SLC22A5, but also exhibited developmental regression and cystic leukoencephalopathy, and an additional diagnosis of complex I deficiency was suspected.
evidence.explanation: Both diagnoses in one sentence, in the order they were made, which is what makes the attribution unambiguous.

open_questions/1.rationale:
Because it belongs to a different disease in the same patient.
The first of the two 2018 patients was initially diagnosed with primary systemic carnitine deficiency on the strength of a homozygous SLC22A5 variant, and the complex I deficiency was suspected only afterwards, when her developmental regression and cystic leukoencephalopathy did not fit. She therefore has two molecular diagnoses, and her low carnitine is attributable to the first.
This matters because the HPO annotation set for OMIM:618235 includes decreased circulating carnitine concentration, sourced to that patient. Curating it from the HPOA row would import a dual-diagnosis confound into the knowledge base as an NDUFA2 phenotype, and it would then be indistinguishable from an observed feature of the disease in any export. It is not curated here.
The general point is worth keeping: in a four-patient entity, one patient's second diagnosis is a quarter of the apparent phenotype. Any future NDUFA2 phenotype claim that traces to this individual needs the SLC22A5 caveat stated in the same breath.

evidence.snippet: Biallelic variants in nuclear gene NDUFA2 have been reported so far in only three children with variable presentations including Leigh syndrome or leukoencephalopathy.
evidence.explanation: The size of the published series, which is the reason there is no natural history to curate.

open_questions/2.rationale:
No, and very little.
Nothing disease-modifying exists for NDUFA2 deficiency, no treatment or response is reported for any of the four patients, and no trial is registered for the gene or the disorder. The one intervention in the literature, baculovirus complementation of patient fibroblasts, is an experiment establishing causality and is curated where it belongs, under experimental_models with a RESCUES link and its limitations attached. This entry therefore has no treatments block.
Supportive management of mitochondrial disease, and the management recommendations in the GeneReviews Leigh syndrome spectrum chapter, are both ready-made content that would look right here. Importing either would assert of four NDUFA2 patients an experience recorded only of other people with other genotypes, and in an exported graph the borrowed annotation would be indistinguishable from an observed one.
Natural history is thinner than the progression block may suggest. What exists is three single-patient courses and one death, and two of the three are known only as an age at last evaluation. There is no age-of-onset distribution, no survival estimate and no imaging series. Closing that needs no new science - a follow-up report on the four published patients would do it.

evidence.snippet: Subject 1 harbored two heterozygous variants within NDUFA6 (GenBank: NM_002490.5; OMIM: 602138), a c.191G>C transversion predicted to cause a p.Arg64Pro missense substitution and a c.265G>T transversion predicted to cause a premature stop codon, p.Glu89∗.
evidence.explanation: The two alleles in the first and most severely affected patient, with full nomenclature.

evidence.snippet: Subject 2 was found to harbor a homozygous 2 bp deletion, c.331_332del, predicted to cause a p.Glu111Serfs∗35 frameshift, whereas subject 3 harbored a homozygous c.3G>A transition predicted to cause the abolition of the initiation methionine (p.?).
evidence.explanation: The two homozygous alleles, including the start-loss variant that later needs its own caveat.

evidence.snippet: None of the subjects’ NDUFA6 variants are reported in the homozygous state in gnomAD, consistent with a very rare status and offering preliminary support for a deleterious etiology.
evidence.explanation: The population-database argument, at the strength the authors give it - preliminary support rather than proof.

evidence.snippet: The c.331_332del variant harbored by subject 2 occurs within the terminal exon of the gene and is therefore predicted to evade nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.
evidence.explanation: Why one frameshift allele is not a simple null at the transcript level, which the genetic_context notes record.

steps/1.description: Two damaged copies of NDUFA6. Six distinct alleles are known across the four children, and they span most of the ways a small gene can be broken. Subject 1 is compound heterozygous for c.191G>C (p.Arg64Pro) and c.265G>T (p.Glu89*); subject 2 is homozygous for the two-base deletion c.331_332del (p.Glu111Serfs*35); subject 3 is homozygous for c.3G>A, which abolishes the initiation methionine; subject 4 is compound heterozygous for the frameshifts c.309del (p.Met104Cysfs*35) and c.355del (p.Leu119Tyrfs*20). None of the six is seen homozygous in gnomAD.

evidence.snippet: Next-generation sequencing identified bi-allelic variants in NDUFA6, encoding a 15 kDa LYR-motif-containing complex I subunit that forms part of the Q-module.
evidence.explanation: Where the protein sits in the enzyme, which sets what its loss can disrupt.

evidence.snippet: This confirmed a marked reduction in incorporated NDUFA6 and a concomitant reduction in other Q-module subunits, including NDUFAB1, NDUFA7, and NDUFA12.
evidence.explanation: The measurement of the subunit's absence from assembled complex I in patient mitochondria.

evidence.snippet: Chromosomal deletion of the corresponding gene in the yeast Yarrowia lipolytica caused concomitant loss of the mitochondrial acyl carrier protein subunit ACPM1 from the enzyme complex and paralyzed ubiquinone reductase activity.
evidence.explanation: The interaction that gives the human observation its meaning, established by deleting the orthologous gene in a yeast. INDIRECT because the claim about the human subunit follows from a non-human system rather than being asserted of it.

steps/2.description: NDUFA6 is an accessory subunit of the Q-module, the ubiquinone-reducing part of the peripheral arm. Complexome profiling of the three patients with available fibroblasts shows a marked reduction of NDUFA6 incorporated into complex I. Its LYR motif is what binds the mitochondrial acyl carrier protein encoded by NDUFAB1, a binding first demonstrated by deleting the orthologous gene in the yeast Yarrowia lipolytica, where loss of the subunit removed ACPM1 from the enzyme and paralysed ubiquinone reductase activity.

evidence.snippet: A loss of NDUFA7 and NDUFA12 from the subcomplex is evident, particularly in subject 1, and appears to correlate with the degree of NDUFA6 loss.
evidence.explanation: The co-loss and its dose relationship with NDUFA6, which is what makes this a consequence rather than a coincidence.

evidence.snippet: It is possible that NDUFA6 is a prerequisite for NDUFA7 and NDUFA12 incorporation into the complex I holoenzyme and that absence of NDUFA6 or its impaired function results in stalling and prevents subsequent interactions with the subunits of the N-module.
evidence.explanation: The mechanistic reading with the hedge the authors put on it, which is why this node is marked PROVISIONAL.

evidence.snippet: this is unsurprising given that the LYR motif of NDUFA6 has been demonstrated to be critical for NDUFAB1 binding in the model aerobic yeast, Yarrowia lipolytica.
evidence.explanation: Why the loss of the acyl carrier protein was expected, and where the expectation came from.

steps/3.description: Losing NDUFA6 takes its neighbours with it. Complexome profiling shows NDUFAB1 lost in the most severely affected patient and markedly reduced in the other two, and NDUFA7 and NDUFA12 lost from the subcomplex in proportion to the degree of NDUFA6 loss. The NDUFAB1 result is the one that was predicted: the LYR motif of NDUFA6 is what binds it. The authors' proposal is that NDUFA6 is a prerequisite for NDUFA7 and NDUFA12 incorporation, which they put forward as a possibility.

evidence.snippet: revealed a reduction of fully assembled complex I levels, whereas all other OXPHOS complexes were unaffected. Complex I subcomplexes, consistent with stalled assembly intermediates, were apparent in the subjects’ cell lines, but not in control cells
evidence.explanation: The assembly defect and the two things that bound it: it is isolated to complex I, and it leaves intermediates that controls do not have.

evidence.snippet: the complexome profiling data provide evidence of NDUFAF2, a late-stage complex I assembly factor, still bound to the stalled assembly intermediate
evidence.explanation: The assembly factor that fails to leave, which is what identifies the stall point.

evidence.snippet: supports the theory that dissociation of NDUFAF2 represents a key checkpoint in complex I holoenzyme assembly
evidence.explanation: What the retention means for assembly generally, stated as support for a theory rather than as a finding.

steps/4.description: Assembly proceeds and then stops. Blue native electrophoresis of patient mitochondria shows reduced fully assembled complex I with subcomplexes present that are absent from controls, and complexome profiling identifies the stall point: an approximately 830 kDa intermediate consisting of the P- and Q-modules but lacking the N-module, with the late assembly factor NDUFAF2 still bound to it. NDUFAF2 retention has previously been seen when the N-module subunits NDUFV1 and NDUFS4 are mutated, and it is the observation behind the idea that NDUFAF2 release is a checkpoint in holoenzyme assembly. All other OXPHOS complexes were unaffected, which is what makes the deficiency isolated.

evidence.snippet: subject complexome data support an ability of the 830 kDa intermediate (plus bound NDUFAF2) to participate in supercomplex formation, whereby fully assembled complexes III and IV appear in complex with the P- and Q-modules of complex I
evidence.explanation: That the incomplete enzyme still enters supercomplexes, which is the surprising part.

evidence.snippet: does not represent a functional respirasome given its apparent lack of NADH dehydrogenase activity
evidence.explanation: Why supercomplex incorporation is not a compensation, in the authors' own terms, and with the hedge (apparent) they attach to it.

steps/5.description: The stalled 830 kDa intermediate, with NDUFAF2 still attached, nonetheless assembles into supercomplexes with fully formed complexes III and IV. That is not a rescue. The resulting particle has no NADH dehydrogenase activity and is therefore not a functional respirasome, which the authors take as evidence that N-module subunits are not needed as scaffolding for supercomplex assembly.

evidence.snippet: Respiratory-chain analyses of muscle biopsy confirmed isolated complex I deficiency in subjects 1 and 2 (44% and 46% of control subjects, respectively)
evidence.explanation: The quantified muscle deficiency in the two patients in whom it was found.

evidence.snippet: revealed a marked reduction in the steady-state levels of complex I subunits for subject 1, whereby the N module and Q module subunits were most affected
evidence.explanation: Which modules of the enzyme are depleted in the most severely affected patient, which is the protein-level counterpart of the complexome result.

steps/6.description: The biochemical endpoint the entity is named for, and it is not uniform. Muscle respiratory-chain analysis showed isolated complex I deficiency at 44 and 46 percent of control in subjects 1 and 2, but normal complex I enzymology in subject 3's muscle despite a marked isolated assembly defect in his fibroblasts - a combination the authors describe as most unusual. Steady-state levels of complex I subunits were reduced in all three patients studied, most markedly in subject 1, with the N-module and Q-module subunits the worst affected.

evidence.snippet: revealed a remarkable impairment of intact cell respiration in subject 1
evidence.explanation: The respiratory defect in the most severely affected patient's cells.

evidence.snippet: Intact cell respiration of subjects 2 and 3 was almost comparable to that of control fibroblasts
evidence.explanation: The negative in the two less severely affected patients, recorded so that impaired respiration is not read as a universal feature of cells carrying these variants.

evidence.snippet: a clear growth defect was demonstrated when glucose-rich culture medium was replaced with galactose-rich (and glucose-free) medium, forcing the cells to be dependent upon oxidative phosphorylation for ATP production
evidence.explanation: The stress test that unmasks a defect in the patient whose basal respiration and muscle enzymology were both normal.

steps/7.description: The cellular consequence, and it is graded in a way that matches the clinical course rather than the genotype. High-resolution respirometry of intact fibroblasts showed a remarkable impairment in subject 1, the child who died at 51 hours, while subjects 2 and 3 were almost comparable to controls. Subject 3's cells nonetheless failed to grow when glucose was replaced by galactose, which forces cells onto oxidative phosphorylation - so his respiratory reserve is reduced even where his basal respiration is not.

evidence.snippet: Initial cranial MRI showed extensive and progressive disseminating lesions in supratentorial white-matter regions, including U-fibers and the corpus callosum, in the basal ganglia, brainstem, and cervical spinal cord, some of which enhanced with contrast
evidence.explanation: The fullest single description of the lesion in the series, in subject 2.

evidence.snippet: MRI shortly after presentation identified white-matter changes especially in the corticospinal tract, brain stem, and thalamus.
evidence.explanation: The same class of lesion in the fourth patient, who died at 13 weeks.

evidence.snippet: White matter abnormalities and/or basal ganglia lesions have been seen on brain imaging.
evidence.explanation: The expert panel's summary of the imaging phenotype across the series. Graded OTHER because a curation narrative is an expert synthesis rather than a study.

steps/8.description: The tissue lesion, and it is imaged rather than examined. All four children had neuroradiological abnormality, but the distribution differs. Subject 1 had diffusely abnormal supratentorial white matter with brainstem and cerebellar white-matter signal change at 36 hours of age. Subject 2 had extensive progressive lesions of supratentorial white matter including the corpus callosum, together with basal ganglia, brainstem and cervical cord involvement, later showing partial cystic degeneration and white-matter volume loss. Subject 3 had increased T2 signal in the basal ganglia with a diffuse atrophic process on follow-up. Subject 4 had white-matter change in the corticospinal tract, brainstem and thalamus.

evidence.snippet: Lactic acidosis exhibited relentless progression with a blood lactate reading in excess of 20 mM immediately before death at approximately 51 hr of age.
evidence.explanation: The terminal course in the first patient, where the acidosis was the lethal event.

evidence.snippet: Routine laboratory investigations revealed normal lactate levels in blood (1.2 mmol/L; normal < 2.2 mmol/L) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (1.8 mmol/L; normal < 2.4 mmol/L).
evidence.explanation: The patient in whom systemic lactate was normal, recorded so that a normal lactate is not read as excluding the diagnosis.

steps/9.description: Three of the four children had raised lactate, and in two it was the proximate cause of death. Subject 1's blood lactate rose from 5.9 to over 20 mmol per litre before she died at about 51 hours. Subject 4's blood gas lactate ran between 16.9 and 18.5 with a CSF lactate of 10.9, and her acidosis was unrelenting to death at 13 weeks. Subject 3 had persistently elevated CSF lactate at 5.0 and later 5.6 mmol per litre. Subject 2 is the exception, with normal lactate in both blood and cerebrospinal fluid - though magnetic resonance spectroscopy did show elevated lactate in multiple brain areas.

evidence.snippet: Respiratory-chain analyses of muscle biopsy confirmed isolated complex I deficiency in subjects 1 and 2 (44% and 46% of control subjects, respectively)
evidence.explanation: The measurement, with the residual activity figures.

evidence.snippet: the situation for subject 3—normal enzymatic activity in muscle despite a demonstrable complex I assembly defect—is most unusual
evidence.explanation: The patient who contradicts the phenotype, in the authors' own words. Recorded as REFUTE against the claim that this finding is general to the disease, which is why the band is FREQUENT rather than OBLIGATE.

steps/10.description: Isolated complex I deficiency in muscle at 44 and 46 percent of control in subjects 1 and 2. Subject 3 is the informative exception: normal complex I enzymology in muscle despite a marked isolated assembly defect in his fibroblasts.

evidence.snippet: Lactic acidosis exhibited relentless progression with a blood lactate reading in excess of 20 mM immediately before death at approximately 51 hr of age.
evidence.explanation: The acidosis and its lethal course in the first patient.

evidence.snippet: Despite intensive-care management in a tertiary care center, her lactic acidosis continued until her death at 13 weeks of age.
evidence.explanation: The same course in the fourth patient, despite tertiary intensive care.

steps/11.description: Metabolic acidosis driven by lactate, and the immediate cause of death in the two infants who died. Subject 1 had a capillary pH of 7.12 with lactate 5.9 mmol per litre within an hour of birth, rising above 20 before death at about 51 hours. Subject 4's blood pH fell from 7.308 to 7.076 with blood gas lactate of 16.9 to 18.5 mmol per litre, and the acidosis continued to her death at 13 weeks.

evidence.snippet: Repeat blood analyses revealed clotting abnormalities, hyperammonaemia (129 μM; normal < 100 μM), and a rising blood lactate (9.3 mmol/L; normal < 2.2 mmol/L).
evidence.explanation: The rising blood lactate in the first patient, with the laboratory's reference interval.

evidence.snippet: Investigation of his seizure disorder revealed elevated CSF lactate (5.0 mmol/L; normal < 2.4 mmol/L) and increased T2 signal in the basal ganglia on cranial MRI.
