edges/22.description: Severe midface hypoplasia narrows or occludes the posterior nasal apertures, producing choanal atresia or stenosis.

edges/23.description: Summary edge: ectopic mineral deposition within the brain is the intracranial calcification phenotype, typically periventricular and involving the basal ganglia and corpus callosum.

edges/24.description: Summary edge: the same ectopic mineralization process deposits mineral in soft tissue and solid organs of longer-surviving patients.

evidence.snippet: a profound failure of dental enamel formation leading to a distinctive hypoplastic AI in all teeth should alert clinicians to the possibility of FAM20C mutations.
evidence.explanation: Directly states that the enamel formation failure leads to the hypoplastic AI phenotype.

edges/25.description: Failed enamel matrix mineralization presents clinically as hypoplastic amelogenesis imperfecta affecting all teeth.

evidence.snippet: Proteomic analysis of differentially expressed proteins demonstrated that proteins involved in extracellular matrix (ECM) regulation and related to the TGFβ/SMAD signaling pathway were increased.
evidence.explanation: Links activated TGF-beta signaling to increased ECM-regulatory protein expression in patient gingiva.

edges/26.description: Activated gingival fibroblasts overproduce and disorganize extracellular matrix.

evidence.snippet: gingival fibrosis and calcifications are associated with, and most likely caused by excessed ECM production and disorganization
evidence.explanation: Attributes the clinical gingival overgrowth phenotype to the excessive, disorganized ECM produced by activated fibroblasts.

edges/27.description: Fibrotic, calcified expansion of the gingival ECM is the tissue substrate of the gum hyperplasia seen clinically.

evidence.snippet: Sequence analysis of FAM20C, located within the deleted region, in six additional affected subjects revealed four homozygous mutations and two compound heterozygotes.
evidence.explanation: Original identification of FAM20C as the Raine syndrome disease gene.

evidence.snippet: Biallelic mutations in the FAM20C gene, which encodes a Golgi serine/threonine protein kinase that phosphorylates secretory pathway proteins, are responsible for RNS.
evidence.explanation: Confirms biallelic FAM20C variants as the cause of Raine syndrome.

evidence.snippet: FAM20C gene, located on chromosome 7p22.3, spanning ~ 107 kb consists of 10 exons and encodes a protein of 584 amino acids in length. A critical kinase domain resides in its C-terminal, encompassing amino acids 354 to 565
evidence.explanation: Gene structure and kinase-domain location.

evidence.snippet: the position of a nonsense variant in the terminal exon of FAM20C gene, could have had a partial effect on the protein function, thereby resulting in a relatively milder phenotype and extended lifespan.
evidence.explanation: Supports the hypomorphic-allele basis of the extended-lifespan phenotype.

evidence.snippet: We found the classic lethal and milder non-lethal phenotypes. The milder phenotype is defined by a large spectrum ranging from osteonecrosis to osteosclerosis with additional congenital defects or intellectual disability in some cases.
evidence.explanation: Reviews the lethal versus non-lethal FAM20C variant-phenotype spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Raine cases due to whole gene deletion do not seem to have a major difference in the phenotype over those caused by various mutations.
evidence.explanation: Whole-gene deletion produces a phenotype comparable to point variants, consistent with loss of function.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic pathogenic variants in FAM20C at 7p22.3 cause Raine syndrome. The gene spans ~107 kb, consists of 10 exons and encodes a 584-amino-acid Golgi serine/threonine kinase whose critical kinase domain lies in the C-terminus (approximately residues 354-565). Reported alleles include missense substitutions at evolutionarily conserved residues, splice-site changes, nonsense variants, a synonymous splice-disrupting variant, and whole-gene deletions (including a 487-kb 7p22.3 deletion and a chromosome 7 uniparental isodisomy with 7p telomeric microdeletion). Complete loss-of-function alleles are associated with the lethal neonatal presentation, while hypomorphic alleles retaining residual kinase activity or partial function underlie the non-lethal form; a nonsense variant in the terminal exon (c.1680C>A, p.Cys560Ter) has been associated with an extended lifespan. Genotype-phenotype correlation remains imperfect, with marked intrafamilial variability and discordant phenotypes reported for identical genotypes.

evidence.snippet: If Raine syndrome is suspected prenatally the newborn should be admitted at a neonatal intensive care unit as significant respiratory distress is often present immediately after birth.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports planned neonatal intensive care as management.

treatments/0.description: When Raine syndrome is suspected prenatally, delivery should be planned with immediate neonatal intensive care availability because significant respiratory distress is usually present from birth; airway management for choanal atresia/stenosis is the immediate priority. Care remains supportive — there is no disease-modifying therapy.

evidence.snippet: Persistent hypophosphatemic rickets was the most striking endocrinological manifestation, which was scarcely responsive to therapy with phosphate salts and alfacalcidol.
evidence.explanation: Documents the treatment used and its limited efficacy in non-lethal Raine syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Plain X-ray radiography and micro-CT radiography analyses showed that the hPi diet improved the shape and mineral density of the Fam20c-deficient femurs/tibiae, and rescued the growth plate defects in the long bone.
evidence.explanation: Preclinical rationale for phosphate repletion; mouse data only, not established human therapy.

treatments/1.description: Conventional therapy for hypophosphatemic rickets with oral phosphate salts and the active vitamin D analogue alfacalcidol has been used in non-lethal Raine syndrome, but the rickets is reported as scarcely responsive to this regimen.

evidence.snippet: Persistent hypophosphatemic rickets was the most striking endocrinological manifestation, which was scarcely responsive to therapy with phosphate salts and alfacalcidol.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the FGF23-driven phosphate-wasting mechanism as the therapeutic target, with limited response.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Aims to replace the phosphate lost through FGF23-driven renal wasting and support mineralization.

evidence.snippet: This article presents the dental manifestations and extensive restorative and oral surgical intervention of three siblings with hypophosphataemic rickets secondary to Raine Syndrome treated at Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children, a tertiary referral hospital.
evidence.explanation: Describes the restorative and surgical dental management used for these patients.

treatments/2.description: Extensive restorative and oral surgical intervention is required for the dental sequelae of non-lethal Raine syndrome, including hypoplastic amelogenesis imperfecta and spontaneous recurrent abscesses on non-carious teeth.

evidence.snippet: We report on a child who is homozygous for a 487-kb deletion in 7p22.3 that contains FAM20C. Both parents were heterozygous for the deletion.
evidence.explanation: Carrier status of both parents underpins recurrence-risk counseling.

treatments/3.description: Autosomal recessive inheritance with a 25% recurrence risk for siblings; consanguinity is common. Carrier testing and prenatal or preimplantation diagnosis are possible once the familial FAM20C variants are known.

evidence.snippet: transgenic mice expressing the mutant Fam20c found in the lethal (KO;G374R) and nonlethal (KO;D446N) Raine syndrome exhibited osteomalacia without osteosclerotic features.
evidence.explanation: Documents the mouse-human mismatch for the defining osteosclerotic phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Fam20c deficiency in mice does not recapitulate the human disorder, so the underlying pathoetiological mechanisms remain poorly understood.
evidence.explanation: States the model-human mismatch explicitly.

open_questions/0.rationale: Global and tissue-specific Fam20c knockout mice, and transgenic mice expressing lethal (G374R) and non-lethal (D446N) Raine syndrome alleles, consistently develop hypophosphatemic rickets or osteomalacia without osteosclerosis. Only occasional conventional knock-in mice show an osteosclerotic radiographic appearance, and micro-CT of those bones shows reduced mineral density and increased porosity. Human autopsy histology likewise shows severe osteomalacia rather than true hypermineralization. This raises the possibility that human "osteosclerosis" is a radiographic semblance superimposed on an underlying osteomalacic/rachitic process, driven by extraskeletal systems (or FAM20C substrates outside bone) not captured by the mouse models.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with RNS can have developmental delay, intellectual disability, seizures, and structural brain defects, but little is known about FAM20C brain-target-protein dysregulation or about a potential pathogenesis associated with neurologic features.
evidence.explanation: Explicitly states that the pathogenesis of the neurologic features is unknown.

evidence.snippet: Case I presented both severe bilateral hearing loss and a partial unilateral visual loss due to occlusion of the central retinal artery
evidence.explanation: Documents case-level sensory findings with disparate proximate causes and no disease-level mechanism.

open_questions/1.rationale: Intracranial calcification, periventricular gliosis, infarction and leukomalacia co-occur with the neurological phenotypes, but no cited source establishes a causal path from calcification or brain injury to seizures, developmental delay, intellectual disability or microcephaly, and the in silico literature explicitly states that FAM20C brain-target dysregulation is unstudied. The sensory involvement is mechanistically heterogeneous at the case level (severe bilateral hearing loss, auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder, conductive loss from glue ear, and a unilateral visual loss from central retinal artery occlusion), with no unifying mechanism proposed. These phenotypes are therefore left without causal edges rather than wired to the calcification node on inference alone.

evidence.snippet: In addition, he had wormian bones and pyriform aperture stenosis, features that are usually under diagnosed.
evidence.explanation: Documents the minor skeletal features as observed findings without a mechanistic account.

open_questions/2.rationale: These features are consistently documented, but the causal statement the literature offers for the craniofacial phenotype (increased ossification of the skull and facial bones) is made only for the facial features - forehead, proptosis, nasal bridge, midface. No cited source articulates a mechanism for palatal shelf fusion failure, ear position, phalangeal hypoplasia or wormian bones, and the multisuture craniosynostosis case report describes but does not explain premature suture fusion. Rather than extend the over-ossification edge to malformations it is not asserted for, these phenotypes are recorded as a mechanistic gap.

evidence.snippet: The GFRA1 gene encodes a receptor on the Wolffian duct that regulates ureteric bud outgrowth in the development of a functional renal system, and has a putative role in the pathogenesis of Hirschsprung disease.
evidence.explanation: States where the receptor sits and what it controls, which is what this node asserts. The sentence describes protein identity rather than an experiment, so it is graded as background.

evidence.snippet: Ureteric bud outgrowth and branching morphogenesis are controlled by the Ret/Gdnf pathway, which is subject to positive and negative regulation by a variety of factors.
evidence.explanation: Places RET in the same pathway as the GFRA1 receptor bound on this node, and names ureteric bud outgrowth as the step it controls.

evidence.snippet: Once it has formed, the mesenchyme secretes GDNF; this induces the nearby wolffian duct to produce a ureteric bud which invades the metanephrogenic mesenchyme and begins to arborize.
evidence.explanation: Names the metanephric mesenchyme as the source of GDNF and the Wolffian duct as its target, which is the geometry this node describes.

evidence.snippet: These findings strongly support the causal role of GFRA1-inactivating variants for an autosomal recessive, nonsyndromic form of BRA.
evidence.explanation: Human genetic evidence that inactivating this component of the complex causes bilateral renal agenesis.

steps/6.description: GDNF secreted by the metanephric mesenchyme acts on the Wolffian duct through GFRA1, a member of the GDNF receptor family, together with the RET receptor tyrosine kinase. Loss of GFRA1 removes that receptor, so the duct no longer receives the outgrowth signal and the ureteric bud is not induced.

evidence.snippet: Once it has formed, the mesenchyme secretes GDNF; this induces the nearby wolffian duct to produce a ureteric bud which invades the metanephrogenic mesenchyme and begins to arborize.
evidence.explanation: This developmental review describes the GDNF-driven reciprocal induction between the metanephric mesenchyme and the ureteric bud whose failure produces renal agenesis.

evidence.snippet: Ureteric bud outgrowth and branching morphogenesis are controlled by the Ret/Gdnf pathway, which is subject to positive and negative regulation by a variety of factors.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that ureteric bud outgrowth, the step that fails in renal agenesis, depends on the Ret/Gdnf signaling pathway.

evidence.snippet: this event depends on the prior action in the intermediate mesoderm of transcription factors such as Lim-1, Pax-2, Eya-1, and Foxc-1.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the upstream transcription factors (including Pax-2) required for metanephric mesenchyme formation, mutations of which cause renal agenesis/hypodysplasia.

evidence.snippet: This demonstrates that GREB1L plays a major role in early metanephros and genital development in mice and humans.
evidence.explanation: Places GREB1L at the early metanephros step this node describes, which is why it is bound as one of the node genes.

evidence.snippet: Itga8 homozygous knockout in mice is known to result in absence of kidney development.
evidence.explanation: The mouse knockout shows ITGA8 is required for the kidney to develop at all, which is the step this node describes.

steps/7.description: Renal agenesis originates from failure of the reciprocal inductive interaction between the ureteric bud and the metanephric mesenchyme. GDNF secreted by the metanephric mesenchyme signals through the RET receptor tyrosine kinase on the ureteric bud to drive bud outgrowth and branching; loss of GDNF-RET signaling, or of upstream regulators such as PAX2, GREB1L, ITGA8, and FGF20, prevents bud outgrowth or invasion of the mesenchyme, so the metanephros never forms.

evidence.snippet: Reduction in the level of these redundant ligands in the mouse led to premature progenitor differentiation within the niche.
evidence.explanation: The mouse experiment shows that reducing FGF20 and FGF9 exhausts the progenitor pool by premature differentiation, which is the state this node describes.

evidence.snippet: Sufficiency was shown in vitro where Fgf20 or Fgf9 (alone or together with Bmp7) maintained isolated metanephric mesenchyme or sorted nephron progenitors that remained competent to differentiate in response to Wnt signals after 5 or 2 days in culture, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Culture of isolated metanephric mesenchyme and sorted nephron progenitors is the direct support for the bound process, progenitor maintenance in metanephric nephron morphogenesis.

evidence.snippet: Loss of FGF20 in humans, or of both ligands in mice, resulted in kidney agenesis.
evidence.explanation: Connects the progenitor defect to the human outcome this node feeds into.

steps/8.description: FGF20 is a niche ligand that, redundantly with FGF9, keeps nephron progenitors in the metanephric mesenchyme undifferentiated. When FGF20 is lost the progenitor pool differentiates prematurely, so the pool is not maintained and kidney development fails. This node is kept separate from ureteric bud outgrowth failure because FGF20 does not act at that step.

evidence.snippet: Bilateral renal agenesis is almost invariably fatal at birth, and unilateral renal agenesis can lead to future health issues including end-stage renal disease.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the two anatomical forms of absent kidney and their divergent clinical consequences.

steps/9.description: Because the ureteric bud and metanephric mesenchyme fail to form a kidney, the affected side has no functioning renal tissue and no ureter. In unilateral disease the contralateral kidney undergoes compensatory hypertrophy and hyperfiltration; in bilateral disease there is no functional renal mass.

evidence.snippet: Bilateral renal agenesis (BRA) is a lethal diagnosis, specifically meaning that natural survival beyond birth is not expected secondary to pulmonary hypoplasia.
evidence.explanation: Directly links bilateral renal agenesis (via oligohydramnios) to lethal pulmonary hypoplasia, the Potter sequence consequence.

steps/10.description: Fetal urine is the major source of amniotic fluid in the second half of gestation. In bilateral renal agenesis the absence of urine output produces severe oligohydramnios, which mechanically compresses the fetus. The resulting deformation cascade is the Potter sequence: pulmonary hypoplasia (the usual cause of neonatal death), Potter facies, and limb contractures.

evidence.snippet: Fetal intervention via amnioinfusion may promote pulmonary survivorship after birth, but postnatal survival remains poor.
evidence.explanation: The largest contemporary BRA series shows that even with amnioinfusion to restore amniotic fluid, postnatal survival remains poor because of the pulmonary consequences of oligohydramnios.

steps/11.description: Pulmonary hypoplasia from oligohydramnios in bilateral renal agenesis leaves insufficient functional lung tissue for gas exchange, causing respiratory failure that is the proximate cause of death in most affected neonates.

edges/6.description: Failed induction means the metanephros and its collecting system never develop.

edges/7.description: Without a functioning GDNF receptor complex the Wolffian duct does not produce a ureteric bud, so reciprocal induction never begins.

edges/8.description: An exhausted nephron progenitor pool leaves no nephrons to form, so the affected side has no functioning renal tissue.

edges/9.description: In bilateral agenesis, absent fetal urine output leads to oligohydramnios.

edges/10.description: Pulmonary hypoplasia leads to fatal respiratory insufficiency at birth.

evidence.snippet: This demonstrates that GREB1L plays a major role in early metanephros and genital development in mice and humans.
evidence.explanation: Identifies heterozygous GREB1L variants as a cause of bilateral kidney agenesis in humans, supported by a Greb1l knockout mouse with absent kidneys.

evidence.snippet: This study is the first to associate a component of the RAR pathway with renal agenesis in humans.
evidence.explanation: Independently identifies GREB1L (a retinoic-acid-receptor pathway component) as a novel human renal agenesis gene.

genes/0.notes: GREB1L is a retinoic-acid target essential for ureteric bud outgrowth; pathogenic variants cause autosomal dominant renal agenesis and severe CAKUT.

genes/1.notes: RET encodes the receptor tyrosine kinase for GDNF that drives ureteric bud outgrowth; loss-of-function impairs kidney induction.

evidence.snippet: Renal coloboma syndrome (RCS) is a highly variable syndrome characterized by renal and ocular abnormalities. It is associated in about 50 % of cases with mutations of PAX2, a gene encoding a transcription factor required during development.
evidence.explanation: Confirms PAX2 as the transcription-factor gene mutated in renal coloboma syndrome, the spectrum that includes renal hypoplasia/agenesis.

genes/2.notes: PAX2 is a transcription factor required for ureteric bud and nephron development; haploinsufficiency causes renal coloboma syndrome with renal hypoplasia/agenesis.

evidence.snippet: These results demonstrate that mutations of ITGA8 are a genetic cause of bilateral renal agenesis and that, at least in some cases, bilateral renal agenesis is an autosomal-recessive disease.
evidence.explanation: Identifies recessive ITGA8 mutations as a cause of bilateral renal agenesis in humans.

evidence.snippet: Itga8 homozygous knockout in mice is known to result in absence of kidney development.
evidence.explanation: The mouse Itga8 knockout recapitulates absent kidney development, supporting ITGA8's role in renal agenesis.

genes/3.notes: ITGA8 (integrin alpha-8) is required for GDNF expression and ureteric bud invasion of the metanephric mesenchyme; biallelic variants cause renal agenesis/hypodysplasia.

evidence.snippet: Loss of FGF20 in humans, or of both ligands in mice, resulted in kidney agenesis.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that loss of FGF20, which maintains nephron progenitor stemness, causes kidney agenesis in humans.

genes/4.notes: FGF20 supports nephron progenitor survival; biallelic loss-of-function causes bilateral renal agenesis.

evidence.snippet: Two homozygous, putative, loss-of-function variants (p.Arg226* and p.Thr432Profs*) were found in index cases with BRA from two unrelated consanguineous families
evidence.explanation: The discovery report identifies two unrelated consanguineous families with homozygous loss-of-function variants and bilateral renal agenesis.

evidence.snippet: The current study represents a second confirmation report on the causal association of GFRA1 pathogenic variants with lethal nonsyndromic bilateral renal agenesis in humans.
evidence.explanation: An independent consanguineous family replicates the gene-disease association.

evidence.snippet: In the first family with BRA, we identified a homozygous missense variant in GFRA1: c.362A>G; p.(Tyr121Cys), which is predicted to damage the protein structure.
evidence.explanation: A third family extends the allelic spectrum from truncating variants to a damaging homozygous missense variant.

evidence.snippet: To date, pathogenic variants in three genes (ITGA8, GREB1L, and FGF20) have been shown to cause renal agenesis in humans.
evidence.explanation: Records that GFRA1 was the fourth established nonsyndromic renal agenesis gene, after the three this entry already carried. The sentence states the state of the field rather than a result of the study.

genes/5.notes: GFRA1 encodes a member of the GDNF receptor family, on the Wolffian duct, that regulates ureteric bud outgrowth. Biallelic loss-of-function or damaging missense variants cause nonsyndromic bilateral renal agenesis, reported in consanguineous families by three independent studies. GDNFRA is a previous HGNC symbol for this gene.

treatments/0.description: Renal replacement therapy to support survivors of bilateral renal agenesis or those with renal failure; rarely feasible in classic bilateral agenesis given perinatal lethality.

treatments/1.description: Definitive renal replacement for survivors who reach candidacy.

treatments/2.description: Long-term monitoring of blood pressure, proteinuria, and renal function in unilateral renal agenesis to detect and manage chronic kidney disease.

treatments/3.description: Counseling for families with monogenic (autosomal dominant or recessive) renal agenesis to convey recurrence risk and inform reproductive decision-making, particularly for the GREB1L-, RET-, PAX2-, ITGA8-, and FGF20-related syndromic forms.

evidence.snippet: Fetal intervention via amnioinfusion may promote pulmonary survivorship after birth, but postnatal survival remains poor.
evidence.explanation: The largest contemporary BRA series reports serial amnioinfusion as a fetal intervention that may promote pulmonary survivorship, though postnatal survival remains poor.

treatments/4.description: Experimental fetal therapy for isolated bilateral renal agenesis in which serial infusions of fluid into the amniotic cavity restore amniotic fluid volume in an attempt to mitigate the pulmonary hypoplasia caused by oligohydramnios. Postnatal survival remains poor.

evidence.snippet: We show that SCUBE3 acts as a BMP2/BMP4 co-receptor, recruits the BMP receptor complexes into raft microdomains, and positively modulates signaling possibly by augmenting the specific interactions between BMPs and BMP type I receptors.
evidence.explanation: The primary functional demonstration of the co-receptor role, from the gene-discovery cohort study.

evidence.snippet: In vitro functional validation studies demonstrated a variable impact of disease-causing variants on transcript processing, protein secretion and function, and their dysregulating effect on bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the disease variants act through BMP signalling, with variable severity across alleles.

evidence.snippet: membrane-associated SCUBE3 may function as a BMP2/4 coreceptor, attract BMP receptor complexes to raft microdomains, and enhance BMP signaling
evidence.explanation: States the molecular function whose loss initiates the disease.

evidence.snippet: the SCUBE3-N294K mutant protein is expressed on the cell surface, but it does not readily form a complex with the BMP type IA receptor
evidence.explanation: Localizes the defect to receptor engagement rather than to surface delivery, which is the distinction this node draws.

evidence.snippet: the gene is prominently expressed in human primary cultured osteoblasts
evidence.explanation: Expression profiling that explains why a ubiquitously available secreted co-receptor produces a skeletal phenotype: the gene is concentrated in the cell type that fails. Trimmed to the human cultured-osteoblast clause so the item carries one kind of evidence; the mouse long-bone half of the same sentence would be model-organism data.

steps/1.description: Biallelic inactivating SCUBE3 variants remove a membrane-associated BMP2/4 co-receptor. Wild-type SCUBE3 attracts BMP receptor complexes to lipid-raft microdomains and enhances BMP signalling, apparently by facilitating the interaction of BMP ligands with BMP type I receptors. The best-characterized illustration of what that loss costs at the protein level is the N294K substitution, which reaches the cell surface normally but fails to complex with BMP type IA receptor - so the defect is in receptor engagement, not in protein trafficking. Read that as mechanism rather than as a patient variant: N294K is a mouse ENU-induced allele and is not among the human variants this entry curates. It is informative here because it sits in the cbEGF7 calcium-binding repeat, the same module the human missense alleles disrupt.

evidence.snippet: whose transcript expression is restricted to the tooth germ epithelium during the development of embryonic mouse teeth, has been demonstrated to play a crucial role in the regulation of tooth development
evidence.explanation: Places SCUBE3 in the tooth germ epithelium during odontogenesis, which is what makes an epithelial-to-mesenchymal instruction the right model here.

evidence.snippet: the specific knockout of SCUBE3 leads to a decrease in height, increase in width of ameloblasts, and loss of representative Tomes processes
evidence.explanation: The ameloblast side of the dental defect in the Scube3 knockout. Two caveats travel with it. Ameloblasts are epithelial, not the mesenchyme-derived odontoblasts this node is bound to, so it supports the node's dental scope rather than its cell type; ameloblast induction is a prerequisite for odontoblast differentiation, which is why it sits here. And the sentence is this paper's introduction reporting somebody else's knockout result rather than its own finding, so the primary report would be the better citation if it can be identified.

steps/2.description:
The dental arm of the mechanism, which is separable from the bone arm rather than a restatement of it. Scube3 transcript in the developing tooth is epithelial, and the protein moves to the mesenchyme, so the defect is in an epithelial-to-mesenchymal instruction: without it, dental mesenchymal cells fail to differentiate into polarized odontoblasts. The epithelial side is affected too - Scube3 knockout ameloblasts are shorter and wider and lose their Tomes processes; ameloblasts are epithelial rather than the mesenchyme-derived odontoblasts this node is bound to, and are recorded here because ameloblast induction is a prerequisite for odontoblast differentiation. This is why dental anomalies are prominent enough to appear in the disorder's ISDS row rather than being an incidental finding.

One caveat on how much this node claims. Nothing has been measured in SCUBE3-deficient human or mouse teeth at the odontoblast level: the Scube3 knockout reports dental defects clinically, and the odontoblast step is a sufficiency result in healthy cells read in reverse. The DECREASED modifiers on the two GO processes are therefore an inference from the direction of those experiments rather than a measured reduction.

evidence.snippet: Scube3-/- mice showed craniofacial and dental defects, reduced body size, and defective endochondral bone growth due to impaired BMP-mediated chondrogenesis and osteogenesis, recapitulating the human disorder.
evidence.explanation: The knockout phenotype from the primary study, explicitly described as recapitulating the human disorder.

evidence.snippet: our analysis of this knockout mouse revealed that it has impaired BMP-mediated chondrogenesis and osteogenesis, which result in craniofacial and dental abnormalities, decreased body size, and faulty endochondral bone development
evidence.explanation: The knockout phenotype, matching the human findings across all four domains.

steps/3.description: Reduced BMP signalling impairs chondrogenesis and osteogenesis. Scube3 knockout mice show impaired BMP-mediated chondrogenesis and osteogenesis with craniofacial and dental abnormalities, decreased body size and faulty endochondral bone development - the same combination of skeletal, facial and dental findings seen in patients, which is what makes this a convincing mechanism rather than a plausible one.

evidence.snippet: 18 affected people from nine independent families who shared the same phenotype of unusual craniofacial features, short stature, skeletal deformities and dental abnormalities
evidence.explanation: Defines the shared clinical phenotype across the discovery cohort.

steps/4.description: The clinical endpoint: reduced growth with a distinctive craniofacial appearance, dental anomalies and skeletal features.

evidence.snippet: the same phenotype of unusual craniofacial features, short stature, skeletal deformities and dental abnormalities
evidence.explanation: Short stature is part of the shared phenotype across nine families.

evidence.snippet: The patient exhibited prenatal growth retardation, short stature, microcephaly, distinctive facial traits
evidence.explanation: Prenatal onset in a molecularly confirmed case - the feature that places this disorder among the primordial dwarfisms.

evidence.snippet: distinctive facial traits, such as long face, high arched eyebrows, epicanthus, blepharoptosis, hypotelorism, high nasal bridge, micrognathia, and large ears
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the facial gestalt in a molecularly confirmed case.

steps/7.description: Reported features include a long face, high-arched eyebrows, epicanthus, blepharoptosis, hypotelorism, a high nasal bridge, micrognathia and large ears.

evidence.snippet: short stature, skeletal deformities and dental abnormalities
evidence.explanation: Dental anomalies are part of the shared phenotype across the discovery cohort.

steps/8.description: Prominent enough to be named in the disorder's ISDS row, and reproduced in the Scube3 knockout mouse - unusual among the group-21 disorders, most of which have no dental component.

evidence.snippet: skeletal abnormalities, including scoliosis, eleven pairs of ribs, mild radial bowing
evidence.explanation: Skeletal findings in a molecularly confirmed case.

evidence.snippet: prenatal growth retardation, short stature, microcephaly, distinctive facial traits
evidence.explanation: Microcephaly in a molecularly confirmed case; curated OCCASIONAL because it comes from a single report rather than the cohort description.

evidence.snippet: skeletal abnormalities, including scoliosis, eleven pairs of ribs, mild radial bowing, irregular endplates in the lower thoracic vertabrae, and narrow iliac wings
evidence.explanation: Long-bone shape abnormality in a molecularly confirmed case, consistent with the defective endochondral bone growth this entry curates.

steps/11.description: Described as mild in the reported case.

evidence.snippet: skeletal abnormalities, including scoliosis, eleven pairs of ribs, mild radial bowing, irregular endplates in the lower thoracic vertabrae, and narrow iliac wings
evidence.explanation: Vertebral endplate irregularity in a molecularly confirmed case.

steps/12.description: Reported in the lower thoracic spine. The endplate is a growth-plate equivalent for the vertebral body, so an irregular endplate is the radiological signature of the same chondro-osseous defect that produces the long-bone findings, rather than a separate lesion.

evidence.snippet: skeletal abnormalities, including scoliosis, eleven pairs of ribs, mild radial bowing, irregular endplates in the lower thoracic vertabrae, and narrow iliac wings
evidence.explanation: Pelvic finding in a molecularly confirmed case.

evidence.snippet: SCUBE3 levels increase significantly during early osteogenic differentiation of hBMSCs, and that reducing SCUBE3 levels can hinder this differentiation
evidence.explanation: A loss-of-function manipulation in human osteogenic precursors, which is the same direction as the disease. Supports the edge rather than either node: removing SCUBE3 is what impairs the differentiation.

evidence.snippet: we demonstrated that disease-associated mutations are associated with reduced transactivation of Smad signaling in vitro
evidence.explanation: Ties the disease alleles specifically to reduced SMAD transactivation, which is the signalling step this edge asserts.

evidence.snippet: By integrating results with a human clinical exome database, we identified a patient with undiagnosed skeletal disease who harbored recessive mutations in SCUBE3
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the alleles assayed above are the human recessive ones, which is what lets the in-vitro result stand for the human disease. Split from the in-vitro clause because the two halves of that sentence are different kinds of evidence.

edges/1.description: Loss of the co-receptor lowers BMP/SMAD output in the cells that build cartilage and bone. Two independent lines make this edge rather than the nodes alone: knocking SCUBE3 down in human bone-marrow mesenchymal stem cells blocks osteogenic differentiation, and the disease-associated alleles themselves reduce SMAD transactivation in vitro.

evidence.snippet: In hDPSCs, exogenous SCUBE3 promoted cell proliferation and migration via TGF-β signalling and accelerated odontoblastic differentiation via BMP2 signalling.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that SCUBE3 acts on odontoblastic differentiation through BMP2. Graded INDIRECT because it is a sufficiency result in healthy cells: the edge's claim that losing SCUBE3 impairs the step follows by inference, not from this experiment.

edges/2.description: The dental arm of the same co-receptor loss. Scube3 is a tooth-germ epithelial transcript, and epithelium-derived SCUBE3 drives odontoblastic differentiation of dental mesenchyme through BMP2 signalling.

evidence.snippet: Scube3-/- mice showed craniofacial and dental defects, reduced body size, and defective endochondral bone growth due to impaired BMP-mediated chondrogenesis and osteogenesis, recapitulating the human disorder.
evidence.explanation: The quoted sentence states the causal direction this edge asserts - the organism-level findings arise from the impaired chondrogenesis and osteogenesis, not merely alongside it.

edges/4.description: Reported in a molecularly confirmed case. Grouped here because cranial bone growth shares the osteogenic defect, but a neural growth mechanism has not been shown.

edges/5.description: Long-bone shape abnormality attributed to the defective endochondral bone growth shown in the knockout. The human finding is a single case report, so the link is inferred from the shared chondro-osseous defect rather than demonstrated.

edges/6.description: The vertebral endplate is a growth-plate equivalent, so its irregularity is read as the vertebral expression of the same chondro-osseous defect. Inferred from a single case report, not demonstrated.

edges/7.description: The ilium forms by endochondral ossification, so its narrowing is attributed to the same defect. Inferred from a single case report, not demonstrated.

evidence.snippet: Scube3-/- mice showed craniofacial and dental defects, reduced body size, and defective endochondral bone growth due to impaired BMP-mediated chondrogenesis and osteogenesis, recapitulating the human disorder.
evidence.explanation: Removing Scube3 produces dental defects, which is the direction this edge asserts. The cited sentence names the clinical-level outcome, not the odontoblast step, so the cell-level attribution rests on the node's own evidence rather than on this quote.

evidence.snippet: exogenous SCUBE3 promoted cell proliferation and migration via TGF-β signalling and accelerated odontoblastic differentiation via BMP2 signalling
evidence.explanation: Graded INDIRECT because the experiment is the converse of the disease: it shows SCUBE3 is sufficient to drive odontoblastic differentiation in healthy human cells, from which the edge infers that losing it impairs that step.

edges/8.description: Failure of polarized odontoblast differentiation is the cellular event behind the clinical dental findings.

evidence.snippet: Scube3-/- mice showed craniofacial and dental defects, reduced body size, and defective endochondral bone growth due to impaired BMP-mediated chondrogenesis and osteogenesis, recapitulating the human disorder.
evidence.explanation: The reduced body size in the knockout is attributed to the same endochondral bone defect, which is the step this edge asserts.

edges/9.description: The growth endpoint of impaired BMP-driven endochondral bone formation.

edges/10.description: Prenatal arm of the same growth deficit.

evidence.snippet: Scube3-/- mice showed craniofacial and dental defects, reduced body size, and defective endochondral bone growth due to impaired BMP-mediated chondrogenesis and osteogenesis, recapitulating the human disorder.
evidence.explanation: Craniofacial defects arise in the knockout from the same impaired chondrogenesis and osteogenesis this node summarizes.

edges/11.description: Craniofacial consequence, reproduced as craniofacial abnormality in the Scube3 knockout mouse.

evidence.snippet: Scube3-/- mice showed craniofacial and dental defects, reduced body size, and defective endochondral bone growth due to impaired BMP-mediated chondrogenesis and osteogenesis, recapitulating the human disorder.
evidence.explanation: Dental defects accompany the skeletal defects in the knockout, from the same BMP-dependent mechanism.

edges/12.description: Dental consequence, also reproduced in the knockout mouse - BMP signalling is required for tooth development as well as bone. The cell-level step is curated separately as Impaired BMP-Driven Odontoblast Differentiation, which also feeds this phenotype.

evidence.snippet: we report a mouse model of skeletal disease, including severe spine deformity, caused by recessive mutation in Scube3
evidence.explanation: An independent recessive Scube3 allele produces spine deformity, which is the causal claim this edge makes rather than a co-occurrence.

evidence.snippet: screening of mouse ENU-induced mutagenesis phenotypes led to the identification of recessive mutations in Scube3 on chromosome 17qA3.3 that confer severe spine deformity, skeleton abnormalities, and altered bone metabolism
evidence.explanation: The review's account of the same ENU result, which is the source the node description was drawing on.

edges/13.description: Axial skeletal consequence; the Scube3 ENU mutant alleles cause spine deformity including severe kyphosis.

evidence.snippet: The discovered variations, which comprised missense, frameshift, nonsense, and canonical splice site modifications as well as a complicated intragenic rearrangement, were dispersed throughout the entire coding sequence of SCUBE3.
evidence.explanation: Characterizes the variant spectrum, which is dispersed rather than domain-restricted.

evidence.snippet: Protein modeling using AlphaFold3 revealed disruption of a critical disulfide bridge within the seventh epidermal growth factor-like repeat, likely affecting protein stability.
evidence.explanation: Structural modelling of a novel missense allele. Classified COMPUTATIONAL because the mechanism claim rests on modelling rather than an assay, and the source hedges it as "likely".

genes/0.notes: SCUBE3 (6p21.31) encodes a secreted and membrane-associated glycoprotein of the SCUBE family. Reported disease variants are missense, frameshift, nonsense, canonical splice-site changes and a complex intragenic rearrangement, dispersed across the whole coding sequence. Several missense variants cluster in the calcium-binding EGF-like repeats, where they disrupt disulfide bonds or calcium coordination and so impair the protein-protein interactions those domains mediate.

evidence.snippet: mice that are homozygous for the tm1(KOPM)Vlcg allele (Scube3−/−) are born at expected Mendelian ratios, show no overt embryonic phenotypes, and are both viable and fertile
evidence.explanation: The half of the mismatch that concerns the mouse: the null is viable, fertile and grossly normal at birth.

evidence.snippet: mouse Scube3 does not appear to affect the HH pathway, unlike zebrafish scube3
evidence.explanation: Sources this discussion's own caveat against itself: the redundancy argument is carried from a Hedgehog result in zebrafish to a BMP claim in mammals, and this sentence is why that step is not safe.

evidence.snippet: Individual functional characterisation has proved challenging because of overlapping expression patterns and compensatory mechanisms that likely obscure specific roles.
evidence.explanation: States the compensation problem the redundancy explanation rests on. Graded OTHER because the sentence describes the difficulty of the research rather than reporting a zebrafish result, and INDIRECT because it is the premise of the argument rather than a demonstration of it.

evidence.snippet: all three Scube proteins contribute to muscle development at distinct levels, with triple knockout zebrafish larvae displaying near-complete Hedgehog loss-of-function phenotypes
evidence.explanation: The concrete demonstration that removing one family member understates the pathway's role, which is the argument for why the single mouse null is mild. Note this is a Hedgehog readout, not BMP.

open_questions/0.rationale: This is a mismatch in severity rather than in kind: the knockout does reproduce the craniofacial, dental and endochondral domains, so the model is informative, but it does not reproduce how much they cost the organism. The standing explanation is redundancy with the other SCUBE family members, and the zebrafish work makes that concrete - single scube mutants are mild while triple mutants approach a complete Hedgehog loss-of-function phenotype. That explanation has a consequence for interpreting this disease, which is why it is worth recording rather than filing as a caveat: if compensation by SCUBE1 and SCUBE2 sets how severe a given individual is, then the variable expressivity in patients may be modifier-driven rather than allele-driven, and no study has tested that. Note also that the zebrafish result is Hedgehog, not BMP, and mouse Scube3 does not affect Hedgehog - so the redundancy argument is being carried across species and across pathways, and it has not been shown for BMP in mammals.

evidence.snippet: In 5/9 families from group 2b, variants were found in TTC37, SCUBE3, NSD2, RABGAP1, and 17p13.3 microdeletions.
evidence.explanation: Places SCUBE3 outside the GH-IGF-I axis group in the only cohort that sorted short-stature genes by that axis, which is the basis for the expectation stated above.

open_questions/1.rationale: The treatments section is empty on purpose. A PubMed search for SCUBE3 with growth hormone, treatment, or management returns no interventional study, no case series reporting a growth response, and no management guideline, and there is no GeneReviews chapter for this gene. Management is presumed symptomatic - orthopaedic care for the spine, dental care, growth monitoring - but nothing supports a treatment entry with a citation, so none is curated. The question is not idle: this disorder is reached through short stature clinics, where recombinant growth hormone is the default question, and the disease mechanism gives a reason to expect it to disappoint. The lesion is in the growth plate's response to BMP rather than in the GH-IGF-I axis, and the cohort that found SCUBE3 explicitly sorted it out of the GH-IGF-I subgroup. That is a mechanistic prediction, not a finding, and it is recorded here so it is not mistaken for one.

open_questions/2.rationale: This entry curates ten phenotypes, and the four skeletal ones added most recently come from a single case report's radiology. That is a strange shape, and the reason is worth recording rather than leaving to be rediscovered. The deep-research reports carry a fuller list with HPO identifiers and denominators - brachydactyly and dental crowding at roughly 80% (12/15), pointed chin ~85%, short palm ~80%, short long bone ~55%, enamel hypoplasia ~27%, and recurrent conductive hearing loss - all of which are more frequent than what is curated here. None was added, because the numbers come from HPO disease annotations rather than from a sentence in a reference this repository can cache, and the abstract of the discovery cohort (PMID:33308444) gives only the four domain headings. So the choice was between verifiable content and coverage, and this entry took verifiability. Closing this needs the full text of PMID:33308444, or the HPO annotation file treated as a citable source in its own right - which would also settle the cardiac and rib-number questions recorded separately here.

open_questions/3.rationale: The bound disease label ends "with or without cardiac anomalies", and this entry curates no cardiac phenotype. The reason is a cache limit, not a finding. The discovery cohort's abstract (PMID:33308444) lists reduced growth, skeletal features, craniofacial appearance and dental anomalies and no cardiac involvement, and its full text is not retrievable into references_cache, so nothing quotable exists either way. Two independent deep-research runs against different providers both report atrial septal defect in two of the cohort and patent foramen ovale in two, attributing it to HPO annotations on OMIM:619184; agreement between them is weak evidence because both are reading the same annotation set rather than the paper. Resolving this needs the full text of PMID:33308444 or the HPO annotation file cited as a source in its own right. Until then the phenotype is absent from this entry, and its absence should not be read as a negative finding.

evidence.snippet: bound to transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) type II receptor through the C-terminal CUB domain, activated TGF-β signaling and triggered the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). This process includes the induction of Smad2/3 phosphorylation
evidence.explanation: Establishes the TGF-beta arm as a real biochemical activity of SCUBE3. Graded INDIRECT because it was shown in lung cancer cells: it supports the existence of the arm this question is about, not its operation in the growth plate.

evidence.snippet: treatment with recombinant human SCUBE3 (rhSCUBE3) protein boosted BMP2 and TGF-β expression, activated mitophagy in hBMSCs, ameliorated oxidative stress, and restored osteogenic function through SMAD phosphorylation
evidence.explanation: Both pathways move together in a skeletal cell type, and the study does not separate them. That is what leaves the question open rather than answering it.

open_questions/4.rationale: This entry models the disorder as a BMP co-receptor loss, which is what the disease literature demonstrates. SCUBE3 also has a separate, well characterized TGF-beta activity: its C-terminal CUB domain binds TGF-beta type II receptor directly and induces SMAD2/3 phosphorylation, so SCUBE3 is a ligand there rather than a co-receptor, and the downstream SMAD branch is a different one. That work was done in lung cancer cells, which is why it is a question here rather than a pathophysiology node - the same molecular interaction in a growth plate would be a different claim. Two observations keep it open. Recombinant SCUBE3 raises both BMP2 and TGF-beta in human bone-marrow mesenchymal stem cells and restores osteogenesis through SMAD phosphorylation, without the two branches being separated; and the SCUBE3-overexpressing transgenic mouse develops cardiac hypertrophy through TGF-beta1, showing the arm is active in vivo in a mammal. Nobody has asked which branch the skeletal phenotype needs.

evidence.snippet: skeletal abnormalities, including scoliosis, eleven pairs of ribs, mild radial bowing, irregular endplates in the lower thoracic vertabrae, and narrow iliac wings
evidence.explanation: The single report of the finding this question is about.

evidence.snippet: SCUBE3 protein exhibits significant expression in various tissues, including primary osteoblasts, long bones, and the cartilage of the axial skeleton throughout development, while also playing a regulatory role in the FGF, Hedgehog, and TGF-β signaling pathways.
evidence.explanation: Axial-skeleton cartilage expression throughout development is what makes an earlier patterning role worth asking about rather than dismissing.

open_questions/5.rationale: Every other skeletal feature in this entry follows from defective endochondral bone growth, which acts on bones that already exist. Rib number does not: it is fixed by axial patterning during somitogenesis, well before the growth plate forms, so the curated mechanism does not reach it. Two readings are open. Either SCUBE3 has an earlier patterning role that nobody has looked for - BMP signalling does act in somite patterning, and mouse Scube3 is expressed in the cartilaginous condensations of ribs and vertebrae - or the finding is incidental. The second reading is the weaker one: a deep-research report puts eleven rib pairs at roughly 31% (4/13) of the cohort, which is recurrent rather than incidental, though that figure comes from HPO annotations and is not quotable in this entry. Settling it needs published rib counts across the reported cohort. Eleven rib pairs is also reported in SSFSC1, the BMP2-related disorder that shares this disease's naming series, which would fit a shared BMP-pathway patterning effect if it holds up.

evidence.snippet:
Biochemical analysis and whole-exome sequencing identified mutations in the 
Golgi-localized UDP-galactose transporter SLC35A2 that define an undiagnosed 
X-linked congenital disorder of glycosylation (CDG) in three unrelated families. 
Each mutation reduced UDP-galactose transport
evidence.explanation: Establishes reduced Golgi UDP-galactose transport as the core molecular defect.

evidence.snippet:
we developed a robust and 
reliable biochemical assay to assess SLC35A2-dependent UDP-galactose transport 
activity in primary fibroblasts. Finally, we show that transport activity is 
directly correlated to the ratio of wild-type to mutant alleles in fibroblasts 
from affected individuals.
evidence.explanation: Functional fibroblast assays confirm reduced UDP-galactose transport that scales with mutant allele burden.

steps/0.description: Pathogenic variants in SLC35A2 reduce transport of UDP-galactose, the nucleotide-sugar donor for galactosylation, from the cytosol into the lumen of the Golgi apparatus (and endoplasmic reticulum for one splice isoform). SLC35A2 is the single known Golgi-localized UDP-galactose transporter, so loss of its activity is the primary biochemical lesion.

evidence.snippet:
An abnormal serum 
N-glycoprofile with significantly increased levels of agalactosylated 
(Hex3HexNAc4-5 and Hex3HexNAc5Fuc1) and monogalactosylated (Hex4HexNAc4 ± 
NeuAc1) N-glycans was observed.
evidence.explanation: Documents the hypogalactosylation signature of N-glycans characteristic of the disorder.

evidence.snippet:
Each mutation reduced UDP-galactose transport, leading to galactose-deficient 
glycoproteins.
evidence.explanation: Directly links reduced transport to galactose-deficient (hypogalactosylated) glycoproteins.

steps/1.description: Reduced lumenal UDP-galactose limits the addition of terminal galactose to N- and O-glycans, producing truncated, agalactosylated and monogalactosylated glycans and secondary hyposialylation (because sialic acid is normally added onto galactose). This yields a type II (processing) CDG glycosylation signature detectable as agalactosylated/monogalactosylated N-glycans and a type II transferrin isoform profile when present.

evidence.snippet:
Patients present with epileptic encephalopathy, 
developmental disability, growth deficiency, and dysmorphism.
evidence.explanation: Summarizes the dominant neurodevelopmental phenotype resulting from the glycosylation defect.

evidence.snippet:
The majority of affected individuals are primarily characterized 
by varying degrees of neurological impairments with or without skeletal 
abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Confirms neurological impairment as the predominant clinical consequence.

steps/2.description: Defective galactosylation of neural glycoproteins and glycolipids impairs central nervous system development and function, manifesting as developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, severe developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, and brain imaging abnormalities (cerebral atrophy, delayed myelination). The central nervous system is the dominant affected organ system in germline SLC35A2-CDG.

evidence.snippet:
We identified somatic pathogenic SLC35A2 variants in 9/20 
(45%) patients with mosaic rates ranging from 7 to 52%.
evidence.explanation: Establishes frequent brain somatic SLC35A2 mosaicism as the genetic basis of MOGHE.

evidence.snippet:
MOGHE is 
histopathologically characterized by clusters of increased oligodendroglial cell 
densities, patchy zones of hypomyelination, and heterotopic neurons in the white 
matter.
evidence.explanation: Describes the cell types and histopathology of the MOGHE lesion.

evidence.snippet: Histopathologically, MOGHE demonstrates subtle cortical dyslamination, heterotopic neurons in the white matter, hypomyelination, and a distinctive increase in the density and clustering of oligodendroglial cells, features that distinguish it from other malformations of cortical development such as focal cortical dysplasia (FCD).
evidence.explanation: A 2026 review restates the defining histopathology and, importantly, what separates MOGHE from FCD.

evidence.snippet: Clinically, the epilepsies associated with MOGHE are heterogeneous, with infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (IESS) being the most common manifestation.
evidence.explanation: Identifies infantile epileptic spasms syndrome as the dominant clinical presentation of this subtype.

steps/3.description: Post-zygotic somatic SLC35A2 variants arising in a neuroglial progenitor during brain development cause brain-restricted mosaicism that underlies mild malformation of cortical development with oligodendroglial hyperplasia in epilepsy (MOGHE) and other malformations of cortical development. MOGHE is characterized by clusters of increased oligodendroglial cell density, patchy hypomyelination, and heterotopic neurons in white matter, and presents as drug-resistant focal epilepsy or early epileptic encephalopathy with epileptic spasms.

evidence.snippet:
Pathogenic de novo variants in the X-linked gene SLC35A2 encoding the major 
Golgi-localized UDP-galactose transporter required for proper protein and lipid 
glycosylation cause a rare type of congenital disorder of glycosylation
evidence.explanation: Establishes SLC35A2 as the causal gene with de novo X-linked variants.

evidence.snippet:
Biochemical analysis and whole-exome sequencing identified mutations in the 
Golgi-localized UDP-galactose transporter SLC35A2
evidence.explanation: Original gene discovery establishing SLC35A2 as the cause.

evidence.snippet:
Oral D-galactose supplementation results in clinical and 
biochemical improvement in SLC35A2-CDG. Galactose supplementation may partially 
overcome the Golgi UDP-galactose deficiency and improves galactosylation.
evidence.explanation: Pilot interventional study demonstrating clinical and biochemical benefit of D-galactose supplementation.

evidence.snippet:
The effect of dietary galactose supplementation on glycosylation was investigated, showing a nearly 
complete normalization of transferrin glycosylation.
evidence.explanation: Earlier case demonstrating biochemical (glycosylation) normalization with galactose supplementation.

evidence.snippet:
Global responder rate was 9/12 (6/6 in 
SLC35A2-positive).
evidence.explanation: Pilot precision-medicine trial showing D-galactose response in SLC35A2-positive MOGHE patients after epilepsy surgery.

treatments/0.description: Oral D-galactose supplementation (dose-escalated up to 1.5 g/kg/day) is an investigational targeted dietary therapy that may partially overcome the Golgi UDP-galactose deficiency and improve galactosylation. A pilot study of 10 patients showed improvements in clinical severity (Nijmegen Pediatric CDG Rating Scale), growth, development, gastrointestinal symptoms, and epilepsy, with improved glycosylation and good tolerability.

evidence.snippet:
All patients had infantile onset epilepsies that were completely or partly resistant 
to multiple anti-epileptic medications or ketogenic diet.
evidence.explanation: Documents use of antiseizure medications, often with incomplete response.

treatments/1.description: Symptomatic management of epilepsy, although infantile-onset seizures are frequently resistant to multiple antiseizure medications and ketogenic diet.

evidence.snippet:
We describe clinical, 
genetic, neuroimaging, EEG, and histopathologic findings and assess possible 
predictors of postoperative seizure and cognitive outcome in 47 patients with 
refractory epilepsy and brain somatic SLC35A2 gene variants
evidence.explanation: Surgical cohort assessing postoperative seizure outcomes in brain somatic SLC35A2 epilepsy.

treatments/2.description: For drug-resistant focal epilepsy associated with brain somatic SLC35A2 variants (MOGHE), surgical resection of the epileptogenic lesion can achieve seizure freedom in a majority of patients.

open_questions/0.rationale: SLC35A2 supplies UDP-galactose to every galactosyltransferase in the Golgi, so the default reading is that all galactosylated glycoconjugates are affected together and the brain is simply the most sensitive tissue. A 2026 forebrain-knockout study reports something narrower - a specific defect in O-GalNAc glycan synthesis with other galactose-containing glycoconjugates intact, truncated precursors accumulating on extracellular matrix molecules, and a correlation between variant burden and glycan truncation in human epilepsy tissue. If that holds, the therapeutic target and the biomarker both change, and galactose supplementation would be expected to work only insofar as it repletes the O-GalNAc branch. The finding is a preprint and has not been reproduced, so this entry does not yet curate a dedicated O-GalNAc node.

evidence.snippet: Markedly decreased succinyl-CoA synthetase activity due to a deleterious mutation in SUCLA2, the gene encoding the beta subunit of the ADP-forming succinyl-CoA synthetase ligase, was found in muscle mitochondria of patients with encephalomyopathy and mtDNA depletion.
evidence.explanation: Enzyme deficiency in patient muscle mitochondria in the discovery kindred.

evidence.snippet: The mechanism of disease is loss of function.
evidence.explanation: ClinGen expert-panel statement of disease mechanism.

evidence.snippet: On the basis of our model, all previously described mutations were predicted to result in decreased amounts of incorrectly assembled protein or disruption of ADP phosphorylation, explaining the severe early lethal manifestations.
evidence.explanation: Structural modelling of the known alleles predicts loss of assembled protein or catalytic function.

steps/1.description: Biallelic SUCLA2 variants remove or inactivate the beta subunit of the ADP-forming succinyl-CoA synthetase (A-SUCL). Splice, nonsense, frameshift, whole-gene and intragenic deletions and missense alleles are reported. Missense alleles such as p.Arg407Trp and p.Asp333Gly are associated with milder or slowly progressive disease.

evidence.snippet: In cultured cells, the p.M329V resulted in a reduced amount of the SUCLA2 protein, impaired production of mitochondrial ATP, and enhanced production of reactive oxygen species
evidence.explanation: Reduced mitochondrial ATP production in cells carrying a patient allele.

steps/2.description: Loss of A-SUCL removes the succinyl-CoA to succinate step with its coupled ATP formation. This is a direct metabolic consequence, independent of mtDNA copy number, and is the step that succinate supplementation was designed to bypass. In patient cells carrying p.Met329Val, mitochondrial ATP production was impaired and reactive oxygen species production enhanced.

evidence.snippet: The mtDNA depletion may be explained by the interaction of succinate-CoA ligase with nucleoside diphosphate kinase, which is involved in mitochondrial nucleotide metabolism.
evidence.explanation: Review synthesis of the NDPK hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: Our data also suggest that the deregulation of mitochondrial nucleoside diphosphate kinase (NDPK) together with defects in mitochondrial transcription factors including mitochondrial DNA pol γ and Twinkle contribute to SCS A-β deficiency-mediated mtDNA instability.
evidence.explanation: In cultured mouse neurons with SUCLA2 knockdown, NDPK deregulation accompanies mtDNA instability.

evidence.snippet: We have investigated this relationship by studying SUCLA2 deficient fibroblasts derived from patients and detected normal mtDNA content and normal NDPK activity.
evidence.explanation: In patient fibroblasts, SUCLA2 loss does not reduce NDPK activity or mtDNA, so the mechanism is not cell-autonomous in every cell type.

evidence.snippet: However, knockdown of SUCLG2 by shRNA in both patient and control fibroblasts resulted in a significant decrease in mtDNA amount, decreased NDPK and cytochrome c oxidase activities, and a marked growth impairment.
evidence.explanation: Removing the complementing SUCLG2 isoform unmasks NDPK and mtDNA loss, consistent with isoform complementation explaining tissue specificity.

steps/3.description: A-SUCL physically associates with mitochondrial NDPK, which forms the nucleoside triphosphates used for mtDNA synthesis; SUCLA2 is described as stabilising NDPK. Loss of the association is the favoured explanation for mtDNA depletion. The evidence is indirect: NDPK activity and mtDNA content were normal in SUCLA2-deficient patient fibroblasts, whereas knockdown of the GTP-forming partner SUCLG2 in the same cells lowered both, suggesting that SUCLG2 complements SUCLA2 loss in cells that express it. In SUCLA2-knockdown mouse neurons, deregulated NDPK was among the changes accompanying mtDNA loss.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show that succinyl-CoA accumulates in cells derived from patients with recessive mutations in the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA) gene succinyl-CoA ligase subunit-β (SUCLA2), causing global protein hyper-succinylation.
evidence.explanation: Measured in patient fibroblasts and myotubes.

steps/4.description: Succinyl-CoA builds up behind the block. Two consequences follow: backflow through the propionate pathway, and non-enzymatic succinylation of lysine residues across the proteome.

evidence.snippet: Defects in SUCLA2 can be found at the metabolite level and are defined by mildly elevated methylmalonic acid and C4-dicarboxylic carnitine concentrations in body fluids in association with variable lactic acidosis.
evidence.explanation: Defines the metabolite signature.

evidence.snippet: Elevated levels of MMA were observed in embryonic brain.
evidence.explanation: The mouse model reproduces the methylmalonic acid elevation in brain.

steps/5.description: Succinyl-CoA excess inhibits methylmalonyl-CoA conversion, so methylmalonic acid and C4-dicarboxylic (methylmalonyl- and succinyl-) carnitine rise in body fluids. The elevation is mild compared with classical methylmalonic acidemia and may be marginal or absent in urine; plasma methylmalonic acid is more consistently raised. Methylcitrate is also raised.

evidence.snippet: the ratio of mtDNA to nuclear DNA, determined by real-time PCR, was reduced to 32% of the mean control value. The mtDNA:nuclear DNA ratio in fibroblasts was 95% of the mean control value.
evidence.explanation: Muscle depletion with normal fibroblast mtDNA in the discovery family.

evidence.snippet: The defect could be convincingly shown at the protein level and our data also confirm the previously described mitochondrial DNA depletion.
evidence.explanation: Confirms mtDNA depletion in the Faroese and Italian series.

evidence.snippet: Mutant placenta and embryonic (e17.5) brain, heart and muscle showed varying degrees of mtDNA depletion (20-60%). However, there was no mtDNA depletion in mutant liver, where the gene is not normally expressed.
evidence.explanation: In the Sucla2 gene-trap mouse, depletion follows the tissues that express Sucla2.

evidence.snippet: mtDNA content could be restored by reintroduction of Sucla2.
evidence.explanation: Rescue in mutant fibroblasts ties the depletion to Sucla2 loss.

evidence.snippet: A-SUCL is mainly expressed in testis, brain and skeletal muscle tissue, whereas G-SUCL is expressed in liver and anabolic tissues
evidence.explanation: Tissue distribution of the two isoforms, consistent with brain and muscle involvement and liver sparing.

evidence.snippet: The mitochondrial DNA contents in skeletal muscle (SM) were normal in both siblings.
evidence.explanation: Depletion is absent in some patients despite the typical phenotype.

evidence.snippet: We studied two families, with children manifesting with slowly progressive mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, hearing impairment and transient methylmalonic aciduria, without mtDNA depletion.
evidence.explanation: A milder allele (p.Asp333Gly) causes disease without mtDNA depletion.

steps/6.description: Reduced mtDNA copy number in skeletal muscle (and, in the mouse model, brain), with normal copy number in fibroblasts and in liver, where SUCLA2 is not the dominant isoform. In the discovery family muscle mtDNA was 32% of control and fibroblast mtDNA 95%. Depletion is not obligatory: siblings with normal muscle mtDNA and a family with a slowly progressive course without depletion have been reported, so the respiratory chain defect can arise without measurable depletion. The GTP-forming SUCLG2 isoform, expressed in liver and anabolic tissues, is thought to protect tissues that express it.

evidence.snippet: Using mass spectrometry, we quantify nearly 1,000 protein succinylation sites on 366 proteins from patient-derived fibroblasts and myotubes.
evidence.explanation: Proteome-wide hypersuccinylation in patient cells.

steps/7.description: Excess succinyl-CoA succinylates lysines on nearly a thousand sites in patient cells, many of them targets of the NAD+-dependent desuccinylase SIRT5. In the forebrain knockout mouse, hypersuccinylation is associated with reduced complex I activity and altered chromatin and neuronal gene expression; in sucla2 mutant zebrafish it consumes NAD+ and propagates respiratory defects. This is an emerging mechanism, established in patient cells and animal models but not yet in patient tissue.

evidence.snippet: The activities of complexes I and IV were significantly decreased, and complexes III and V were less affected, whereas complex II, the only complex that does not contain mtDNA-encoded proteins, was borderline normal
evidence.explanation: Muscle respiratory chain pattern in the discovery family.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of respiratory chain enzyme activities in muscle generally showed a combined deficiency of complexes I and IV, but normal histological and biochemical findings in muscle did not preclude a diagnosis of succinate-CoA ligase deficiency.
evidence.explanation: The pattern across the 71-patient review, and its limits.

evidence.snippet: Here, by down-regulating the expression levels of SCS A-β in cultured mouse neurons, we have found that SCS A-β deficiency induces severe mitochondrial dysfunction including lowered oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) efficiency, increased mitochondrial superoxide production, and mtDNA depletion as well as aberrations of mitochondrial fusion and fission proteins, which eventually leads to neuronal stress.
evidence.explanation: Reduced OXPHOS and increased superoxide in SUCLA2-knockdown neurons; supports the oxidative arm of the conformed module node in vitro.

steps/8.description: Reduced activity of complexes I and IV (with III and V less affected) and borderline-normal complex II in muscle, the pattern of a defect in mtDNA-encoded subunit synthesis. Normal muscle histology and enzymology do not exclude the diagnosis. Increased reactive oxygen species production is shown in patient cells and knockdown neurons, not in patient tissue.

evidence.snippet: Our work establishes that SUCLA2 is expressed exclusively in neurons in the human cerebral cortex.
evidence.explanation: Neuronal localisation of SUCLA2 in human surgical cortex.

evidence.snippet: Clinically the diagnosis should be considered in patients with early/neonatal onset encephalomyopathy, dystonia, deafness and Leigh-like MRI abnormalities mainly affecting the putamen and the caudate nuclei.
evidence.explanation: The basal ganglia pattern.

evidence.snippet: Neuroimaging showed demyelination and central and cortical atrophy, including atrophy of the basal ganglia, and some of the patients fulfilled the criteria for Leigh syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Imaging in the 12-patient Faroese series.

steps/9.description: Selective injury of the putamen and caudate, seen as Leigh-like T2 hyperintensity and later atrophy, with demyelination and cortical and central atrophy. SUCLA2 is expressed in neurons and not in glia in human cortex. Early MRI can be normal, with abnormalities appearing later, and MR spectroscopy may show lactate when structural imaging is normal.

evidence.snippet: SUCLA2 loss within murine skeletal muscle yields a model of SCS-deficient mitochondrial myopathy with reduced body weight, muscle weakness and exercise intolerance.
evidence.explanation: Muscle-autonomous consequence of Sucla2 loss.

steps/10.description: Skeletal muscle weakness and atrophy. A muscle-specific Sucla2 knockout mouse shows growth failure, reduced grip strength and exercise intolerance, with the oxidative soleus more affected than the glycolytic extensor digitorum longus.

evidence.snippet: SUCLA2-related mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome, encephalomyopathic form with methylmalonic aciduria (SUCLA2-related mtDNA depletion syndrome) is characterized by onset of the following features in infancy: developmental delay, hypotonia, dystonia, muscular atrophy, sensorineural hearing impairment, growth failure, and feeding difficulties.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews core feature with infantile onset.

evidence.snippet: Patients with SUCLA2 gene defects characteristically develop the trias of early hypotonia, progressive dystonia and sensori-neural deafness.
evidence.explanation: Early hypotonia is part of the characteristic triad in 16 Faroese children.

steps/11.description: Muscular hypotonia from the first months of life, often the presenting sign.

evidence.snippet: SUCLA2-related mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome, encephalomyopathic form with methylmalonic aciduria (SUCLA2-related mtDNA depletion syndrome) is characterized by onset of the following features in infancy: developmental delay, hypotonia, dystonia, muscular atrophy, sensorineural hearing impairment, growth failure, and feeding difficulties.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews core feature.

steps/12.description: Psychomotor delay from infancy, typically severe.

evidence.snippet: Clinical features in affected individuals include LSS, developmental delay and regression, encephalopathy, myopathy, choreoathetosis, dystonia, seizures, ptosis, sensorineural hearing loss, feeding difficulty, failure to thrive, and elevated lactate and methylmalonic acid.
evidence.explanation: ClinGen summary of the curated cases lists regression.

evidence.snippet: Our patients present with an early infantile Leigh-like encephalomyopathy with deafness, and later on a progressive dystonia.
evidence.explanation: Progressive dystonia after infantile onset.

evidence.snippet: We describe a purely neurologic allelic form of the disease consisting of deafness, putamenal hyperintensity on MRI and a myoclonic-dystonic movement disorder unchanging from childhood into, so far, the late fourth decade.
evidence.explanation: Non-progressive allelic form with p.Arg407Trp.

steps/14.description: A hyperkinetic-dystonic movement disorder that follows the early hypotonia and is progressive in the typical form. With the p.Arg407Trp allele a myoclonic-dystonic movement disorder has been reported to remain unchanged from childhood into the fourth decade.

evidence.snippet: Other less frequent features include choreoathetosis, muscle weakness, recurrent vomiting, ptosis, and kyphoscoliosis.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews less frequent feature.

evidence.snippet: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and liver involvement was exclusively found in patients with SUCLG1 mutations, whereas epilepsy was much more frequent in patients with SUCLA2 mutations compared to patients with SUCLG1 mutations.
evidence.explanation: Epilepsy is a feature of the SUCLA2 disorder.

steps/16.description: Epilepsy occurs in a minority and is much more frequent with SUCLA2 than with SUCLG1 deficiency.

evidence.snippet: The most frequent abnormality on neuroimaging was basal ganglia involvement, found in 69% of SUCLA2 and 80% of SUCLG1 patients.
evidence.explanation: 69% of SUCLA2 patients (FREQUENT band).

evidence.snippet: Despite the prominent movement disorder, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was normal while 1H-magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) showed lactate peaks in the cerebral cortex and lateral ventricles.
evidence.explanation: A normal MRI does not exclude the diagnosis.

steps/17.description: Leigh-like T2 hyperintensity and atrophy of the putamen and caudate; the most frequent neuroimaging abnormality. Early imaging may be normal.

evidence.snippet: Progressive hearing loss, in combination with a characteristic metabolite profile (increased lactate, methylmalonic acid, C4-dicarboxylic carnitine, 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid) should lead the clinician to the correct diagnosis even in patients with only intermittent lactic acidemia.
evidence.explanation: Progressive hearing loss in 16 Faroese children.

evidence.snippet: The symptoms comprise hypotonia, muscle atrophy, hyperkinesia, severe hearing impairment and postnatal growth retardation.
evidence.explanation: Severe hearing impairment in the 12-patient series.

steps/18.description: Sensorineural hearing loss, often severe and progressive; one of the defining features, and managed with hearing aids or cochlear implantation.

evidence.snippet: The symptoms comprise hypotonia, muscle atrophy, hyperkinesia, severe hearing impairment and postnatal growth retardation.
evidence.explanation: Muscle atrophy as a core symptom.

evidence.snippet: Other less frequent features include choreoathetosis, muscle weakness, recurrent vomiting, ptosis, and kyphoscoliosis.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews less frequent feature.

evidence.snippet: SUCLA2-related mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome, encephalomyopathic form with methylmalonic aciduria (SUCLA2-related mtDNA depletion syndrome) is characterized by onset of the following features in infancy: developmental delay, hypotonia, dystonia, muscular atrophy, sensorineural hearing impairment, growth failure, and feeding difficulties.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews core feature.

steps/21.description: Feeding difficulty in infancy; gastrostomy is used when needed to maintain intake.

evidence.snippet: The symptoms comprise hypotonia, muscle atrophy, hyperkinesia, severe hearing impairment and postnatal growth retardation.
evidence.explanation: Postnatal growth retardation as a core symptom.

evidence.snippet: Other less frequent features include choreoathetosis, muscle weakness, recurrent vomiting, ptosis, and kyphoscoliosis.
